luna-luna-2.casi_fallo: Luna 1, eight months earlier, got its engine burn timing wrong and flew past; Luna 2 repeated the attempt.
luna-luna-2.leccion: To reach the Moon you have to hit the exact instant of the rocket burn.
luna-luna-2.logro: First human-made object to touch another celestial body. It confirmed that the Moon has no appreciable magnetic field or radiation belts.
luna-luna-2.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-luna-2.nota: Impact site unknown; usually given as between ~29-31 N, 1 W to 1 E.

texto.ninos: It was the first thing humans put on the Moon, in 1959. It weighed about as much as five adults and crashed on purpose. Did you know it carried pennants with its country's coat of arms?
texto.org: Luna 2 (1959-014A), impact on Sep 13, 1959 near 30.0 N, 0.0 E; the reported zone spans 29–31 N and 1 W–1 E (NSSDCA code 'a'). First human artefact to reach the lunar surface. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but in little pieces: it hit very fast and nobody has found the exact spot.
faq.org: Yes. The impact site has not been identified in LROC images; the position is approximate (code 'a').

faq.ninos: Because it was the first time something made by people reached another world.
faq.org: First artificial impact on the Moon; its magnetometers and particle instruments detected no lunar magnetic field or radiation belt.

luna-luna-2-etapa-3.objeto: Third stage of the launch vehicle
luna-luna-2-etapa-3.leccion: Whatever pushes a probe towards the Moon usually follows the same path and arrives too.
luna-luna-2-etapa-3.logro: Second human-made object on the Moon; it arrived about 30 minutes after Luna 2.
luna-luna-2-etapa-3.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-luna-2-etapa-3.nota: Third stage of the Luna 2 rocket; it hit ~30 min after Luna 2.

texto.ninos: The rocket that pushed Luna 2 also crashed into the Moon, half an hour later, about as long as a long recess. Nobody knows where it fell. Do you think someone will find it one day?
texto.org: Third stage of the Luna 2 launcher, impact on Sep 13, 1959 about 30 min after the probe; impact site unknown (NSSDCA code 'b'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, somewhere on the Moon, but nobody knows where.
faq.org: Yes; no coordinates have been published and the site has not been identified in orbital images.

faq.ninos: Because it shows that, from the very first trip, we left more things than we count.
faq.org: It is the first case of auxiliary hardware (a rocket stage) abandoned on the Moon, a pattern repeated with the Apollo S-IVB stages.

luna-ranger-4.casi_fallo: The onboard computer failed shortly after launch and the probe was left out of control.
luna-ranger-4.leccion: A single component can make a whole mission useless; more testing on the ground is needed.
luna-ranger-4.logro: First US object to reach the Moon, although it sent no data. It fell on the far side.
luna-ranger-4.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-ranger-4.nota: Coordinates from Siddiqi (2002, 2018) and Ulivi and Harland (2004).

texto.ninos: This probe 'fell asleep' on the way and crashed on the side of the Moon we never see from Earth. It weighed about as much as four adults. What could be there, on the far side?
texto.org: Ranger 4 (1962-012A), impact on Apr 26, 1962 at 15.5 S, 130.7 W, far side (NSSDCA code 'c', Siddiqi/Ulivi-Harland). Central computer failure; it returned no data. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but on the other side of the Moon, where it is hard to look.
faq.org: Yes; the far-side site has not been identified by LROC and the coordinates are approximate.

faq.ninos: Because it was the first thing from its country to reach the Moon, even though it did not work.
faq.org: First American artefact on the Moon; its failure drove the redesign of the Ranger programme.

luna-ranger-6.casi_fallo: The cameras switched on by accident during launch and burned out; it reached the Moon blind.
luna-ranger-6.leccion: An electrical arc at lift-off can ruin a system that looked intact.
luna-ranger-6.logro: It reached the planned spot in the Sea of Tranquility; its failure led to fixes on the next probe.
luna-ranger-6.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-ranger-6.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: It arrived exactly where it wanted, but its 6 cameras had burned out and it did not send a single photo. It was like arriving at a concert blindfolded. What would you learn from a trip like that?
texto.org: Ranger 6 (1964-007A), impact on Feb 2, 1964 at 9.3864 N, 21.4806 E, Mare Tranquillitatis. Cameras inoperative due to an electrical arc at launch. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes: a camera circling the Moon found the mark it left.
faq.org: Yes; the impact crater was identified in LROC images (code 'd').

faq.ninos: Because crashing on purpose was also the plan: they wanted very close-up photos.
faq.org: It proved the programme's precise navigation; the camera failure was fixed on Ranger 7.

luna-ranger-7.casi_fallo: The six previous Ranger missions had failed; this was the programme's last chance.
luna-ranger-7.leccion: Fixing one failure at a time, patiently, pays off in the end.
luna-ranger-7.logro: First US success at the Moon: more than 4,300 high-resolution images before impact.
luna-ranger-7.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-ranger-7.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: After six failures, this probe sent more than 4,300 photos in just 17 minutes, like taking four photos a second while you fall. Can you imagine the excitement in the control room?
texto.org: Ranger 7 (1964-041A), impact on Jul 31, 1964 at 10.6340 S, 20.6770 W, Mare Cognitum. It transmitted 4,308 TV images before impact. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes, you can see the small crater it made when it hit.
faq.org: Yes; the impact crater was identified in LROC images (code 'd').

faq.ninos: Because its photos showed for the first time what the Moon's ground looks like up close.
faq.org: Its images, with resolution down to ~0.5 m, were key to choosing Apollo landing sites.

luna-ranger-8.logro: More than 7,000 images of the Sea of Tranquility, the region where Apollo 11 landed four years later.
luna-ranger-8.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-ranger-8.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: It sent more than 7,000 photos of the place where, years later, the first astronauts would walk. It was like sending a scout to check the yard before the party. What would you look for in those photos?
texto.org: Ranger 8 (1965-010A), impact on Feb 20, 1965 at 2.6376 N, 24.7881 E, Mare Tranquillitatis. 7,137 images transmitted. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes, the crater it left shows up in photos from orbit.
faq.org: Yes; impact site identified by LROC (code 'd').

faq.ninos: Because it helped choose where Apollo 11 would land.
faq.org: Its oblique images covered the Mare Tranquillitatis area used for Apollo site selection.

luna-ranger-9.logro: Its images of Alphonsus crater were broadcast live on television: 'Live from the Moon'.
luna-ranger-9.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-ranger-9.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: Millions of people watched live on TV as this probe fell into a crater 110 kilometres wide, as wide as a big city. Would you have watched until the end?
texto.org: Ranger 9 (1965-023A), impact on Mar 24, 1965 at 12.8281 S, 2.3884 W, Alphonsus crater. 5,814 images, relayed live. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes, you can see the mark of its crash inside the big crater.
faq.org: Yes; impact crater identified by LROC (code 'd').

faq.ninos: Because it was the first time people watched the Moon coming closer live.
faq.org: Last Ranger; its images of the floor of Alphonsus supported studies of lunar volcanic activity.

luna-luna-5.casi_fallo: The retrorocket did not fire and the probe crashed instead of braking.
luna-luna-5.leccion: Braking in time is as hard as getting there.
luna-luna-5.logro: First Soviet soft-landing attempt; its data served the attempts that followed.
luna-luna-5.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-luna-5.nota: Luna 5 site according to Ksanfomality (2018); other sites have been reported.

texto.ninos: It wanted to set down gently, but its brake did not work. It weighed about as much as a small car and crashed into the Sea of Clouds. What would you do if your brake failed?
texto.org: Luna 5 (1965-036A), impact on May 12, 1965 near 1.35 S, 25.48 W, Mare Nubium; the literature reports several different sites (NSSDCA code 'e', Ksanfomality 2018). Retrorocket failure. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but it is not clear at which point; books give different places.
faq.org: Yes; the coordinates are uncertain and the site is not confirmed in LROC images.

faq.ninos: Because every failed attempt taught something towards the first soft landing.
faq.org: First soft-landing attempt of the E-6 series; it preceded the success of Luna 9.

luna-luna-7.casi_fallo: The retrorocket fired too early and the probe arrived without braking.
luna-luna-7.leccion: The braking moment has to be exact, neither early nor late.
luna-luna-7.logro: Another step in the Soviet learning curve towards the first soft landing.
luna-luna-7.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-luna-7.nota: Coordinates from Siddiqi (2002, 2018) and Ulivi and Harland (2004).

texto.ninos: It braked too early and then fell with no brake into the Ocean of Storms. It was like hitting the brakes 1 kilometre before the traffic light. Why do you think braking at the Moon is so hard?
texto.org: Luna 7 (1965-077A), impact on Oct 7, 1965 near 9 N, 49 W, Oceanus Procellarum (NSSDCA code 'c'). Premature retrorocket ignition. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, although the exact point is approximate.
faq.org: Yes; approximate coordinates from historical sources, with no LROC confirmation.

faq.ninos: Because it shows that getting there first took many attempts.
faq.org: Second consecutive failure of the E-6 series; it provided data to adjust the descent sequence.

luna-luna-8.casi_fallo: The retrorocket fired too late and did not manage to brake.
luna-luna-8.leccion: After failing by being early and by being late, the next attempt got it right.
luna-luna-8.logro: Last failure before Luna 9; it completed the tests of the descent system.
luna-luna-8.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-luna-8.nota: Coordinates from Siddiqi (2002, 2018) and Ulivi and Harland (2004).

texto.ninos: This time the brake fired late. It reached the ground still going several hundred kilometres per hour, like a fast train. How many attempts would you make before giving up?
texto.org: Luna 8 (1965-099A), impact on Dec 6, 1965 near 9.1 N, 63.3 W, Oceanus Procellarum (NSSDCA code 'c'). Late retrorocket ignition. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, in the Ocean of Storms, which is made of rock, not water.
faq.org: Yes; approximate coordinates, not identified in LROC images.

faq.ninos: Because it was the last stumble before the first soft landing in history.
faq.org: Its descent data enabled the success of Luna 9 two months later.

luna-luna-9.casi_fallo: Five earlier probes of the same series had crashed.
luna-luna-9.leccion: A design that cushions the blow, with inflated bags, can achieve what retrorockets alone cannot.
luna-luna-9.logro: First soft landing in history and first photos from the lunar surface. It showed that the ground can support a spacecraft.
luna-luna-9.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-luna-9.nota: Coordinates from an early Soviet report; LROC does not see the lander there (probably 10+ km away).

texto.ninos: It was the first spacecraft to set down on the Moon without breaking, in 1966. It weighed about as much as a large person and sent the first photos from the lunar ground. What would you have wanted to see in that first photo?
texto.org: Luna 9 (1966-006A), soft landing on Feb 3, 1966 at 7.13 N, 64.37 W, Oceanus Procellarum; coordinates from the initial Pravda report, LROC does not find the lander there (NSSDCA code 'f'). First soft landing and first panoramic surface images. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but the cameras in orbit have not found it yet.
faq.org: Yes; the position published in 1966 does not match anything in LROC images, so the real site remains unconfirmed.

faq.ninos: Because it showed that the Moon's ground was not dust you sink into.
faq.org: First soft landing; it ruled out the hypothesis of a deep regolith unable to support a spacecraft.

luna-surveyor-1.casi_fallo: It was the first flight of the design and of the Atlas-Centaur rocket; a high chance of failure was expected.
luna-surveyor-1.leccion: A well-tested design can work the first time.
luna-surveyor-1.logro: First US soft landing; it sent more than 11,000 images and measured the strength of the soil.
luna-surveyor-1.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-surveyor-1.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: It was the first spacecraft from its country to land softly on the Moon, and it did so on the first try. It sent more than 11,000 photos, like a huge album. Which photo would you ask it for?
texto.org: Surveyor 1 (1966-045A), landing on Jun 2, 1966 at 2.4745 S, 43.3398 W, Oceanus Procellarum. 11,237 images transmitted. Lander photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes, it looks like a tiny dot with its long shadow.
faq.org: Yes; the lander and its shadow are identified in LROC images (code 'd').

faq.ninos: Because it confirmed that astronauts could step down without sinking.
faq.org: It validated the leg design and the bearing capacity of the regolith for the Apollo lunar module.

luna-surveyor-2.casi_fallo: One of the three correction engines did not fire and the spacecraft began to tumble out of control.
luna-surveyor-2.leccion: If one engine out of three fails, you need a plan to stay stable.
luna-surveyor-2.logro: Its failure helped improve the engines of the following Surveyors, which did land.
luna-surveyor-2.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-surveyor-2.nota: Coordinates from Siddiqi (2002, 2018) and Ulivi and Harland (2004).

texto.ninos: One of its 3 engines did not fire and the spacecraft began spinning like a top until it crashed. What happens if one leg of a three-legged stool breaks?
texto.org: Surveyor 2 (1966-084A), impact on Sep 22, 1966 near 5.5 N, 12.0 W, southeast of Copernicus crater (NSSDCA code 'c'). A vernier engine failed to ignite during the course correction. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, in pieces near a famous crater.
faq.org: Yes; approximate coordinates, not identified by LROC.

faq.ninos: Because the engineers reviewed the engines and the next five Surveyors worked.
faq.org: The only in-flight failure of the Surveyor vernier system; it prompted reviews for missions 3 to 7.

luna-lunar-orbiter-1.casi_fallo: Overheating and imaging-system problems; many high-resolution photos came out blurred.
luna-lunar-orbiter-1.leccion: It is crashed on purpose at the end so as not to get in the way of the next mission.
luna-lunar-orbiter-1.logro: It took the first photograph of Earth seen from the Moon.
luna-lunar-orbiter-1.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-lunar-orbiter-1.nota: According to Boeing (1968); another reference gives 6.7 N, 162 E.

texto.ninos: It took the first photo of Earth from the Moon, like a selfie of the whole planet. When it finished, it was crashed on purpose to leave the space clear. What would you think on seeing Earth so tiny?
texto.org: Lunar Orbiter 1 (1966-073A), deliberate impact on Oct 29, 1966 at 6.35 N, 160.71 E, far side; other references give 6.7 N, 162 E (NSSDCA code 'h'). First image of Earth from lunar orbit. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: So that it would not collide with the spacecraft that came later.
faq.org: To avoid radio interference and collision risk with later missions of the programme.

faq.ninos: Because it showed us our planet from another world for the first time.
faq.org: It began the orbital mapping that made it possible to choose the Apollo landing sites.

luna-luna-13.logro: Second Soviet soft landing; it measured the hardness and density of lunar soil for the first time with a penetrometer.
luna-luna-13.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-luna-13.nota: Coordinates from Siddiqi (2002, 2018) and Ulivi and Harland (2004).

texto.ninos: It landed on Christmas Eve 1966 and drove a small hammer into the ground to find out how hard it was. It weighed about as much as a large person with a suitcase. How would you measure whether ground is soft?
texto.org: Luna 13 (1966-116A), soft landing on Dec 24, 1966 at 18.87 N, 62.05 W, Oceanus Procellarum (NSSDCA code 'c'). A penetrometer and radiation densitometer measured the mechanical properties of the regolith. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, although the exact place is approximate.
faq.org: Yes; approximate historical coordinates, with no confirmed LROC identification.

faq.ninos: Because it was the first to measure how firm the Moon is to walk on.
faq.org: First in situ measurements of regolith density and strength, before Surveyor 3.

luna-luna-10.leccion: Whatever is left circling the Moon ends up falling, and nobody tracks it.
luna-luna-10.logro: First artificial satellite of the Moon. It measured radiation, micrometeorites and the gravity field.
luna-luna-10.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-luna-10.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: It was the first satellite to circle the Moon, in 1966. It went round more than 450 times, like a runner who does not stop for two months, and then fell somewhere nobody knows. Where do you think it is?
texto.org: Luna 10 (1966-027A), first lunar orbiter; orbit decayed, impact site unknown (NSSDCA code 'g', estimated 1966). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it fell onto the Moon somewhere, but nobody saw it fall.
faq.org: Yes; the orbit decayed untracked and there are no impact coordinates.

faq.ninos: Because it was the first object to orbit another world.
faq.org: First artificial satellite of another body; its gravity data foreshadowed the lunar 'mascons'.

luna-luna-11.casi_fallo: A foreign body jammed the attitude system and the cameras pointed away from the Moon.
luna-luna-11.leccion: A loose part can spoil the most important part of the mission.
luna-luna-11.logro: Second Soviet orbiter; it studied radiation and micrometeorites for 38 days.
luna-luna-11.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-luna-11.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: It circled the Moon 277 times, but its cameras were looking the wrong way. It weighed about as much as a small car and fell somewhere unknown. How would you feel if your camera pointed the wrong way at the big moment?
texto.org: Luna 11 (1966-078A), orbiter; orbit decayed, impact site unknown (NSSDCA code 'g', estimated 1966). An attitude failure prevented useful images from being obtained. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it fell onto the Moon without anyone seeing where.
faq.org: Yes; untracked orbital decay, no impact coordinates.

faq.ninos: Because it is one of the 'ownerless papers': we know it is there, but not where.
faq.org: Early example of an object abandoned in lunar orbit with no record of its fall.

luna-surveyor-3.casi_fallo: The radar did not shut the engines off in time and the spacecraft bounced twice before coming to rest.
luna-surveyor-3.leccion: Parts that come back from the Moon must be handled with maximum cleanliness so they are not mistaken for lunar life.
luna-surveyor-3.logro: The only spacecraft visited by astronauts: Apollo 12 landed next to it and brought its camera back to Earth in 1969.
luna-surveyor-3.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-surveyor-3.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: Two years after it arrived, the Apollo 12 astronauts landed just 160 metres away, about two blocks, and took its camera as a souvenir. Which piece would you take?
texto.org: Surveyor 3 (1967-035A), landing on Apr 20, 1967 at 3.0162 S, 23.4180 W, Oceanus Procellarum. Visited by Apollo 12 in Nov 1969; the camera was recovered. The supposed surviving microbe is now attributed to contamination on Earth (Rummel et al., 2011). Photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Is it true that a bacterium survived on the Moon?
faq.ninos: Probably not: most likely the bacterium slipped in on Earth, when the camera was opened.
faq.org: The hypothesis was seriously questioned in 2011; the most likely explanation is contamination during handling on Earth (source 36).

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes, and you can also see the footprints of the astronauts who visited it.
faq.org: Yes; LROC shows the lander, the Apollo 12 one and the paths between them (code 'd').

luna-surveyor-4.casi_fallo: Contact was lost about 2.5 minutes before touchdown, perhaps because the braking engine exploded.
luna-surveyor-4.leccion: With no signal in the final stretch, nobody knows whether the spacecraft landed or crashed.
luna-surveyor-4.logro: Its sudden silence remains a mystery; the site is only an estimate.
luna-surveyor-4.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-surveyor-4.nota: Surveyor 4 may have broken up; contact was lost ~2.5 min before landing.

texto.ninos: Everything was going well and suddenly, two and a half minutes before arriving, it stopped talking. Nobody knows whether it set down or broke apart. What do you think happened to it?
texto.org: Surveyor 4 (1967-068A), contact lost on Jul 17, 1967 ~2.5 min before touchdown; estimated position 0.5 N, 1.5 W, Sinus Medii, possibly fragmented (NSSDCA code 'i'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Almost certainly yes, but it may be whole or in pieces.
faq.org: Yes; estimates are given for a soft landing and for an impact, with no LROC confirmation.

faq.ninos: Because it is an unsolved mystery on the map of the Moon.
faq.org: The only Surveyor whose fate is undetermined; the probable cause is the rupture of the solid retrorocket.

luna-surveyor-5.casi_fallo: A helium leak left the braking system almost without pressure; a new descent sequence was improvised within hours.
luna-surveyor-5.leccion: A ground team that improvises calmly can save a mission.
luna-surveyor-5.logro: First chemical analysis of lunar soil, with an alpha-scattering instrument: it was basaltic rock.
luna-surveyor-5.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-surveyor-5.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: A leak almost left it without brakes, but the engineers invented a new plan in a few hours and it landed. Then it discovered that the ground was like the cold lava of volcanoes. How would you save a mission in one day?
texto.org: Surveyor 5 (1967-084A), landing on Sep 11, 1967 at 1.4551 N, 23.1943 E, Mare Tranquillitatis. A helium leak forced the descent to be reprogrammed. First in situ chemical analysis (alpha scattering). Photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes, it looks like a bright dot in a small crater.
faq.org: Yes; identified in LROC images (code 'd').

faq.ninos: Because it was the first to tell us what the Moon is made of.
faq.org: It determined the basaltic composition of the regolith, a key fact before Apollo 11.

luna-lunar-orbiter-3.casi_fallo: The motor of the film-processing system failed and some photos were never transmitted.
luna-lunar-orbiter-3.leccion: It is crashed on purpose at the end so as not to get in the way of the next mission.
luna-lunar-orbiter-3.logro: It photographed Surveyor 1 from orbit and confirmed landing sites for Apollo.
luna-lunar-orbiter-3.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-lunar-orbiter-3.nota: According to Boeing (1968); other references give different coordinates.

texto.ninos: From above it managed to see another spacecraft, Surveyor 1, as a tiny dot with a shadow. In the end it was crashed on purpose. Could you find a car in a photo taken from a plane?
texto.org: Lunar Orbiter 3 (1967-008A), deliberate impact on Oct 9, 1967 near 14.3 N, 92.7 W; several references give different coordinates (NSSDCA code 'j'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: To clear the way for the spacecraft that followed.
faq.org: Controlled deorbit at the end of the mission to avoid interference with later missions.

faq.ninos: Because its photos helped choose where the astronauts would step.
faq.org: It confirmed 8 candidate sites for Apollo and obtained the first orbital image of a spacecraft on the surface.

luna-lunar-orbiter-2.leccion: It is crashed on purpose at the end so as not to get in the way of the next mission.
luna-lunar-orbiter-2.logro: It took the famous 'picture of the century' of Copernicus crater, seen at an angle as if from a window.
luna-lunar-orbiter-2.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-lunar-orbiter-2.nota: According to Boeing (1968); other references give different coordinates.

texto.ninos: It took such a beautiful photo of Copernicus crater that it was called 'the picture of the century'. That crater is 93 kilometres across, like the distance between two cities. Which photo of yours would deserve that name?
texto.org: Lunar Orbiter 2 (1966-100A), deliberate impact on Oct 11, 1967 near 3.0 N, 119.1 E, far side; alternative coordinates in several references (NSSDCA code 'j'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: So that it would not be left circling out of control.
faq.org: Controlled deorbit at the end of the photographic mission.

faq.ninos: Because its photos showed what the Moon really looks like, with mountains and shadows.
faq.org: It covered 13 Apollo candidate sites and provided the oblique image of Copernicus from Nov 1966.

luna-surveyor-6.logro: First lift-off from the Moon: it fired its engines and hopped about 2.5 metres to see its own footprints.
luna-surveyor-6.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-surveyor-6.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: It was the first spacecraft to lift off from the Moon, although it only hopped two and a half metres, like a kangaroo jump. That way it could look at the marks it left on the ground. What would you see looking at your own footprints?
texto.org: Surveyor 6 (1967-112A), landing on Nov 10, 1967 at 0.4742 N, 1.4275 W, Sinus Medii. On Nov 17, 1967 it performed the first lift-off from the lunar surface (a hop of ~2.5 m). Photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes, it looks like a tiny dot in the centre of the near side.
faq.org: Yes; identified in LROC images (code 'd').

faq.ninos: Because it showed that an engine can be restarted on the Moon.
faq.org: First restart and lift-off from another body, a relevant test for the Apollo ascent stage.

luna-luna-12.logro: It obtained images of the surface from orbit, which Luna 11 had not managed.
luna-luna-12.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-luna-12.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft did manage to photograph the Moon from above, with details the size of a bus. Afterwards it fell somewhere nobody recorded. How many lost things might there be on the Moon?
texto.org: Luna 12 (1966-094A), photographic orbiter; orbit decayed, impact site unknown (NSSDCA code 'g', estimated 1967). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but we do not know which part of the Moon it fell on.
faq.org: Yes; untracked orbital decay, no impact coordinates.

faq.ninos: Because it is another of the objects with unknown whereabouts that the map must count.
faq.org: First Soviet orbiter with useful images (resolution ~15–20 m), 1966–1967.

luna-lunar-orbiter-4.casi_fallo: Contact was lost on Jul 17, 1967 before its fall could be steered.
luna-lunar-orbiter-4.leccion: If contact is lost, the object falls wherever it likes and nobody records it.
luna-lunar-orbiter-4.logro: It mapped 99% of the near side of the Moon from a polar orbit.
luna-lunar-orbiter-4.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-lunar-orbiter-4.nota: Contact lost on Jul 17, 1967; impact date uncertain (perhaps between 22 and 30 W).

texto.ninos: It photographed almost all of the face of the Moon that we see, 99 percent, like putting together a giant jigsaw puzzle. Then it went silent and fell without anyone knowing where. Would you like to put that puzzle together?
texto.org: Lunar Orbiter 4 (1967-041A); contact lost on Jul 17, 1967, impact date uncertain (1967), estimated longitude between 22 and 30 W, site unknown (NSSDCA code 'k'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, at some point on the Moon that nobody has found.
faq.org: Yes; no published coordinates, only an estimated longitude range.

faq.ninos: Because it made the first almost complete map of the near side.
faq.org: First systematic photographic coverage of the near side from polar orbit.

luna-surveyor-7.casi_fallo: The chemical analysis instrument did not lower by itself and had to be pushed with the mechanical arm.
luna-surveyor-7.leccion: A robotic arm is useful for fixing whatever gets stuck.
luna-surveyor-7.logro: The only Surveyor in the highlands, next to Tycho crater; it detected a laser sent from Earth.
luna-surveyor-7.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-surveyor-7.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: It landed near Tycho crater, in the mountains, and saw a laser beam sent from Earth 380,000 kilometres away, like a million football pitches in a row. Would you see a torch from that far?
texto.org: Surveyor 7 (1968-001A), landing on Jan 10, 1968 at 40.9812 S, 11.5127 W, north rim of Tycho. Last Surveyor; the only mission on highland terrain. Photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: Yes, it can be seen near the rim of a crater with bright rays.
faq.org: Yes; identified in LROC images (code 'd').

faq.ninos: Because it was the only one that studied the Moon's mountains, not the plains.
faq.org: The only pre-Apollo in situ sampling of the highlands; its composition differed from the basaltic maria.

luna-lunar-orbiter-5.leccion: It is crashed on purpose at the end so as not to get in the way of the next mission.
luna-lunar-orbiter-5.logro: It completed the photographic map of the far side and obtained an almost full image of Earth.
luna-lunar-orbiter-5.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.

texto.ninos: It was the last of 5 siblings that photographed the whole Moon from orbit. Together they made the first complete map. When it finished, it was brought down on purpose. Which map would you like to complete?
texto.org: Lunar Orbiter 5 (1967-075A), deliberate impact on Jan 31, 1968 at 2.79 S, 83.04 W; estimated coordinates (NSSDCA code 'l'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: So that it would not get in the way of the Apollo spacecraft that were coming.
faq.org: Controlled deorbit at the end of the mission, common practice for all five Lunar Orbiters.

faq.ninos: Because with it the first map of the whole Moon was finished.
faq.org: With LO 4 and 5, photographic coverage of 99% of the lunar surface was reached.

luna-luna-14.logro: It studied the lunar gravity field and tested communications for future Soviet crewed missions.
luna-luna-14.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-luna-14.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: It circled the Moon measuring how its gravity pulls, which is 6 times weaker than Earth's. Afterwards it fell somewhere nobody knows. How high would you jump on the Moon?
texto.org: Luna 14 (1968-027A), orbiter; orbit decayed, impact site unknown (NSSDCA code 'g', estimated 1968–1969). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but without anyone knowing the place.
faq.org: Yes; untracked orbital decay, no impact coordinates.

faq.ninos: Because it is another lost object that the map must acknowledge.
faq.org: Last probe of the E-6LS series; gravity and communications data for the Soviet crewed lunar programme.

luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.nombre: Descent stage of the lunar module Eagle (Apollo 11)
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.objeto: Lunar module descent stage (LM-5, Eagle) with the laser retroreflector and the seismometer
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.estado: Inactive (descent stage intact on the surface; ascent stage abandoned in lunar orbit, final fate uncertain)
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.casi_fallo: After separation, the service module unexpectedly passed close to the capsule.
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.leccion: Share the lessons and update the reports.
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.logro: First crewed Moon landing. It brought back 21.55 kg of samples and left a laser retroreflector that is still used to measure the Earth–Moon distance.
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.historia: The first crewed vehicle to land on the Moon. It carried commander Neil Armstrong and pilot Buzz Aldrin to the Sea of Tranquility ('Tranquility Base').
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.legado_cientifico: It enabled the first human steps on another world, the collection of about 21.5 kg of lunar samples and the deployment of the EASEP.
luna-apollo-11-lm-descenso.equipo_dejado: Lunar Module descent stage (legs, platform and engine) and the EASEP experiment package next to the laser retroreflector.

texto.ninos: This is where the first people set down on the Moon. They left a special mirror that still bounces back laser beams from Earth, 384,000 kilometres away, like an echo of light that takes 2.5 seconds to return. What would you ask that mirror?
texto.org: Descent stage of LM-5 from AS-506, landing on Jul 20, 1969 at 0.67416 N, 23.47314 E (Mare Tranquillitatis); site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). The LRRR retroreflector remains operational for the ILRS. Sources: NSSDCA, ILRS.

faq.ninos: Yes. You can even see the astronauts' footprints from above.
faq.org: Yes; LROC photographed the stage, the instruments and the footprints. The site is protected by the One Small Step Act (2020).

faq.ninos: On the way back, part of the spacecraft passed very close to the capsule. Luckily they did not collide.
faq.org: The service module, after separation, unexpectedly passed close to the command module; the lesson was to share and update flight reports (Johnson, 2018).

faq.ninos: Yes, the laser mirror. It needs no batteries: it just reflects light.
faq.org: The 100-prism retroreflector is still in use; it allows the Earth–Moon distance to be measured with millimetre precision (ILRS, JPL).

luna-luna-15.casi_fallo: It tried to bring back samples with a robot before Apollo 11; it crashed into a mountain during descent.
luna-luna-15.leccion: The race to get there first can cost the mission.
luna-luna-15.logro: First attempt at robotic sample return, while Armstrong and Aldrin were on the surface.
luna-luna-15.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-luna-15.nota: Same as c; alternative sites are reported for Luna 15.

texto.ninos: It wanted to bring back Moon rocks with a robot, just when the first astronauts were there. It weighed about as much as 4 cars and crashed into a mountain. Who do you think was winning that race?
texto.org: Luna 15 (1969-058A), impact on Jul 21, 1969 near 17 N, 60 E, Mare Crisium; other sources give 12 N, 59 E or 17 N, 49 E (NSSDCA code 'c1'). First sample-return attempt, simultaneous with Apollo 11. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, in pieces, although it is not clear at which point.
faq.org: Yes; several coordinates in the literature, with no LROC confirmation.

faq.ninos: Because it shows that two countries were competing for the Moon on the same day.
faq.org: It illustrates the space race: the USSR sought a robotic return simultaneous with the first crewed landing.

luna-apollo-12-lm-descenso.nombre: Descent stage of the lunar module Intrepid (Apollo 12)
luna-apollo-12-lm-descenso.objeto: Lunar module descent stage (LM-6, Intrepid) and ALSEP station
luna-apollo-12-lm-descenso.casi_fallo: Two lightning strikes at lift-off. John Aaron's "SCE to Aux" recovered the systems.
luna-apollo-12-lm-descenso.leccion: Redundancy on different hardware; weather rules for launching.
luna-apollo-12-lm-descenso.logro: Precision landing 160 m from Surveyor 3. It brought back 34.35 kg of samples and left the first nuclear-powered ALSEP station.
luna-apollo-12-lm-descenso.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-apollo-12-lm-descenso.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-apollo-12-lm-descenso.radiactivo_detalle: ALSEP SNAP-27, ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 oxide

texto.ninos: At lift-off, two lightning bolts hit the rocket and the displays went dark. A young engineer remembered a switch and saved the mission. Then they landed 160 metres from an old probe, like walking a block and a half. Which switch do you know by heart?
texto.org: Descent stage of LM-6 from AS-507, landing on Nov 19, 1969 at 3.0128 S, 23.4219 W (Oceanus Procellarum); site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). ALSEP powered by a SNAP-27 (~3.9 kg of Pu-238). Sources: NSSDCA, NASA RPS.

faq.ninos: Yes, next to the instruments they left and the Surveyor 3 probe.
faq.org: Yes; LROC shows the stage, the ALSEP and the path to Surveyor 3. Site protected by the One Small Step Act.

faq.ninos: Two lightning bolts shut almost everything down at lift-off; an engineer knew what to do.
faq.org: Two discharges at 36 and 52 s after lift-off; John Aaron's "SCE to Aux" call restored telemetry. Lesson: redundancy on different hardware and weather rules.

faq.ninos: It carries a special battery that runs on the heat of a radioactive material, well protected.
faq.org: Yes: SNAP-27 with ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 dioxide, in a graphite cask; the ALSEP worked until 1977.

luna-apollo-12-lm-ascenso.nombre: Ascent stage of the lunar module Intrepid (Apollo 12)
luna-apollo-12-lm-ascenso.casi_fallo: Two lightning strikes at lift-off. John Aaron's "SCE to Aux" recovered the systems.
luna-apollo-12-lm-ascenso.leccion: Redundancy on different hardware; weather rules for launching.
luna-apollo-12-lm-ascenso.logro: First artificial impact recorded by a seismometer on the Moon: the Moon 'rang' for almost an hour.
luna-apollo-12-lm-ascenso.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-12-lm-ascenso.nota: Coordinates estimated from seismic data (Toksoz et al. 1974; Orloff 2000; Wagner et al. 2017).

texto.ninos: This cabin was not lost: it was crashed on purpose so the seismometer could feel the blow. The Moon rang for almost an hour, like a giant bell. What sound do you imagine it made?
texto.org: Ascent stage of LM-6 from AS-507, targeted impact on Nov 20, 1969 at 3.94 S, 21.20 W; coordinates estimated from seismic data (NSSDCA code 'm', Toksöz et al. 1974). Calibrated seismic source for the ALSEP PSE. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Science: the blow was used to listen to what the Moon is like inside.
faq.org: Deliberate impact as a seismic source of known energy; the signal reverberated for ~55 minutes and surprised seismologists.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: It has not been photographed yet; the place was calculated from the quake.
faq.org: Not identified by LROC; the position comes from the seismic network, with an uncertainty of several kilometres.

faq.pregunta: What almost went wrong on Apollo 12?
faq.ninos: Two lightning bolts at lift-off; an engineer knew the right switch.
faq.org: Electrical discharges at launch; "SCE to Aux" restored telemetry. Lesson: redundancy on different hardware and weather rules (Johnson, 2018).

luna-apollo-10-lm-descenso.nombre: Descent stage of the Apollo 10 lunar module
luna-apollo-10-lm-descenso.casi_fallo: When the stages were separated 14 km above the surface, a switch in the wrong position sent the module spinning out of control for a few seconds.
luna-apollo-10-lm-descenso.leccion: Check every switch on the checklist: one small detail changes the whole flight.
luna-apollo-10-lm-descenso.logro: Dress rehearsal for the landing: it descended to 14 km above the Moon without touching it and tested the whole procedure Apollo 11 used two months later.
luna-apollo-10-lm-descenso.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-apollo-10-lm-descenso.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft practised going down to the Moon without landing, like a diver peering over the edge. It came within just 14 kilometres of the surface, the distance of a long bike ride. Where might it have fallen afterwards?
texto.org: Descent stage of LM-4 from AS-505, abandoned in lunar orbit in May 1969; the orbit decayed and the impact site is unknown (NSSDCA code 'g', estimated year 1969). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but nobody knows which part of the Moon it fell on.
faq.org: It hit at an unknown date and site after orbital decay; it has not been identified by LROC.

faq.ninos: Because that mission was only a rehearsal: they wanted to test everything except the last step.
faq.org: Apollo 10 was the full test of the descent profile in lunar orbit; the landing was reserved for Apollo 11.

faq.pregunta: And the other half of the spacecraft?
faq.ninos: The top part went off to circle the Sun and is still out there.
faq.org: The ascent stage (Snoopy) was sent into heliocentric orbit; it is not in the NSSDCA lunar table.

luna-apollo-11-lm-ascenso.nombre: Ascent stage of the lunar module Eagle (Apollo 11)
luna-apollo-11-lm-ascenso.casi_fallo: After separation, the service module unexpectedly passed close to the capsule.
luna-apollo-11-lm-ascenso.leccion: Share the lessons and update the reports.
luna-apollo-11-lm-ascenso.logro: It carried Armstrong and Aldrin back to lunar orbit; it was left there and its final whereabouts are unknown.
luna-apollo-11-lm-ascenso.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-apollo-11-lm-ascenso.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: This cabin lifted the first two astronauts from the Moon up to their spacecraft. Then it was left circling alone and nobody knows where it fell, like a balloon that slips away. Do you think someone will find it one day?
texto.org: Ascent stage of LM-5 from AS-506, abandoned in lunar orbit on Jul 21, 1969; orbit decayed, impact site unknown (NSSDCA code 'g'). Some recent orbital analyses suggest it could still be in orbit, unconfirmed. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Nobody knows for sure: it fell somewhere or is still circling.
faq.org: NSSDCA classifies it as a decayed orbit with unknown impact; it has not been identified by LROC.

faq.ninos: Because it was no longer needed: only the capsule could go home.
faq.org: The mission profile discarded the ascent stage after docking to save mass for trans-Earth injection.

faq.pregunta: What almost went wrong on Apollo 11?
faq.ninos: On the way back, part of the spacecraft passed very close to the capsule.
faq.org: Unexpected close pass of the service module after separation; lesson: update the reports and share lessons (Johnson, 2018).

luna-apollo-13-s-ivb.casi_fallo: Oxygen tank 2 exploded: its switches were rated for 28 V and on the ground they received 65 V. The lunar module served as a lifeboat.
luna-apollo-13-s-ivb.leccion: Have contingency procedures ready; repeat the risk analysis after every design change.
luna-apollo-13-s-ivb.logro: Although the mission did not land, its S-IVB stage was crashed on purpose and the Apollo 12 seismometer recorded the quake: even the failed mission left a scientific data point.
luna-apollo-13-s-ivb.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-13-s-ivb.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This rocket was not lost: it was sent into the Moon on purpose to feel a quake. It was like ringing a giant bell! It weighed almost 14 tonnes, like ten cars together. What might the seismometer have felt?
texto.org: S-IVB from AS-508, impact on Apr 15, 1970 at 2.5550 S, 27.8875 W, recorded by the passive seismometer of the Apollo 12 ALSEP. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Sources: NSSDCA, NASA SVS.

faq.ninos: Yes, it left a crater about 30 metres wide that shows up in photos from orbit.
faq.org: Yes; the ~30 m crater was identified in LROC images (NASA SVS 4803).

faq.ninos: An oxygen tank exploded and the crew used the lunar module as a lifeboat to get back.
faq.org: Failure of O2 tank no. 2: 28 V thermostats subjected to 65 V on the ground; the LM served as a lifeboat (NSSDCA, Review Board Report 1970).

faq.ninos: That you need a plan B ready before something fails.
faq.org: Contingency procedures prepared, and repeat the risk analysis after every design change (Johnson, 2018).

luna-luna-16.objeto: Descent stage of the sample-return probe
luna-luna-16.casi_fallo: The five previous Soviet sample-return probes failed at launch or at the Moon; this was the first to work from start to finish.
luna-luna-16.leccion: A robot can bring back samples without risking anyone; repetition and step-by-step improvement pay off.
luna-luna-16.logro: First robotic sample return from another world: 101 grams of soil from the Sea of Fertility.
luna-luna-16.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-luna-16.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This robot drilled into the Moon and sent 101 grams of lunar dust back to Earth, about the weight of a chocolate bar. Nobody travelled with it: it did everything alone. Can you imagine a machine that brings gifts from the Moon?
texto.org: Luna 16 descent stage, landing on Sep 20, 1970 at 0.5137 S, 56.3638 E (Mare Fecunditatis); the ascent stage returned 101 g of regolith to Earth on Sep 24, 1970. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, the bottom part of the robot stayed on the Moon and a camera in orbit photographed it.
faq.org: Yes. The descent stage remains in Mare Fecunditatis and was identified in LROC images (NSSDCA code 'd').

faq.ninos: It was the first time an uncrewed machine brought little pieces of the Moon to Earth.
faq.org: First robotic sample-return mission; it demonstrated the full landing-drilling-ascent-re-entry chain without a crew.

luna-luna-17.objeto: Landing platform with ramps for the Lunokhod 1 rover
luna-luna-17.casi_fallo: An earlier attempt to take a rover to the Moon (1969) was lost to a rocket failure; Luna 17 was the second attempt.
luna-luna-17.leccion: Separate the platform from the vehicle: if one part fails, the other can be saved.
luna-luna-17.logro: It took to the Moon the first wheeled vehicle to travel across another world and lowered it down two ramps.
luna-luna-17.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-luna-17.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This platform was the garage of a little lunar car: it lowered two ramps and the robot rolled out for a drive. It is in the Sea of Rains, about 380,000 kilometres from your home, like going almost ten times around Earth. Which ramp would the little car choose to roll down?
texto.org: Luna 17 landing platform, landing on Nov 17, 1970 at 38.23764 N, 35.00163 W (Mare Imbrium); it deployed the Lunokhod 1 rover. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, the platform is still sitting in the same place where the little car rolled down the ramp.
faq.org: Yes. The platform remains in Mare Imbrium and appears in LROC images next to the rover's tracks (NSSDCA code 'd').

faq.ninos: Without this garage the first lunar car could never have gone out to explore.
faq.org: It demonstrated the platform-rover concept later used by Chang'e 3 and 4; its coordinates serve as a geodetic reference for the Lunokhod 1 site.

luna-lunokhod-1.objeto: Eight-wheeled exploration vehicle with a laser retroreflector
luna-lunokhod-1.casi_fallo: Its exact position was lost for almost 40 years; in 2010 it was found again in LRO images and its mirror answered the laser once more.
luna-lunokhod-1.leccion: What seems lost can become useful again: a good catalogue of positions is worth as much as the device.
luna-lunokhod-1.logro: First wheeled vehicle on another world: it travelled 10.5 kilometres in 10 months and its laser retroreflector is still in use.
luna-lunokhod-1.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-lunokhod-1.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-lunokhod-1.radiactivo_detalle: Polonium-210 heater to survive the lunar night

texto.ninos: This little car was the first to roll across another world and covered 10.5 kilometres, like crossing a whole city. It was driven from Earth with a steering wheel and it still has a little mirror that bounces back laser beams. Who would want to drive it today?
texto.org: Lunokhod 1 rover (Luna 17), operated from Nov 17, 1970 to Sep 14, 1971 at 38.3150 N, 35.0081 W; it travelled 10.54 km. Located in LROC images (NSSDCA code 'd'); its French laser retroreflector is still used by the ILRS network. Source: NSSDCA, ILRS.

faq.ninos: Yes, and it is not completely asleep: its mirror still bounces back the laser light sent to it from Earth.
faq.org: Yes. It is parked in Mare Imbrium; in 2010 LRO fixed its position and since then its retroreflector has received laser shots from ILRS stations.

faq.ninos: It was the first little car on another world and it still helps measure how far away the Moon is.
faq.org: First planetary rover; its reflector provides Earth–Moon distance measurements with millimetre precision for lunar geodesy and tests of general relativity.

luna-apollo-14-s-ivb.casi_fallo: Docking failed six times; a little ball of solder almost triggered the abort button.
luna-apollo-14-s-ivb.leccion: Anticipate how something can fail and prepare alternatives beforehand.
luna-apollo-14-s-ivb.logro: Impact recorded by the Apollo 12 seismometer: it was used to measure the speed of waves in the lunar crust.
luna-apollo-14-s-ivb.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-14-s-ivb.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This giant rocket, almost 14 tonnes like three elephants, was crashed on purpose. The seismometer from the previous mission felt the blow from 170 kilometres away. What is the point of listening to a quake on the Moon?
texto.org: S-IVB from AS-509, impact on Feb 4, 1971 at 8.1810 S, 26.0305 W, recorded by the PSE of the Apollo 12 ALSEP; site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it left a crater that the cameras in orbit have already photographed.
faq.org: Yes; crater identified in LROC images (code 'd').

faq.ninos: The spacecraft could not latch on: six attempts failed. And a loose little ball of metal almost pressed the abort button by itself.
faq.org: Six failed CSM-LM docking attempts; a ball of solder in the LM panel almost triggered the abort signal, solved with a software patch (Johnson, 2018).

faq.ninos: To imagine what can fail and prepare the solution beforehand.
faq.org: Anticipate failure modes and have alternatives ready before the flight.

luna-apollo-14-lm-descenso.nombre: Descent stage of the lunar module Antares (Apollo 14)
luna-apollo-14-lm-descenso.objeto: Lunar module descent stage (LM-8, Antares), ALSEP and retroreflector
luna-apollo-14-lm-descenso.casi_fallo: Docking failed six times; a little ball of solder almost triggered the abort button.
luna-apollo-14-lm-descenso.leccion: Anticipate how something can fail and prepare alternatives beforehand.
luna-apollo-14-lm-descenso.logro: Landing at Fra Mauro, the destination Apollo 13 did not reach. It brought back 42.28 kg of samples; its retroreflector is still in use.
luna-apollo-14-lm-descenso.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-apollo-14-lm-descenso.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-apollo-14-lm-descenso.radiactivo_detalle: ALSEP SNAP-27, ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 oxide

texto.ninos: This is where the mission landed that completed the trip Apollo 13 could not make. They brought back 42 kilos of rocks, about the weight of a 12-year-old child, and left a laser mirror that still works. Which rock would you take?
texto.org: Descent stage of LM-8 from AS-509, landing on Feb 5, 1971 at 3.64589 S, 17.47194 W (Fra Mauro); site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Retroreflector active in the ILRS; ALSEP with SNAP-27. Sources: NSSDCA, ILRS, NASA RPS.

faq.ninos: Yes, with the laser mirror that still bounces back light from Earth.
faq.org: Yes; stage, ALSEP and retroreflector visible in LROC. The retroreflector remains operational (ILRS).

faq.ninos: The spacecraft would not latch on and a little ball of metal almost pressed the abort button.
faq.org: Six docking failures and a floating ball of solder in the LM abort switch; a software patch was improvised (Johnson, 2018).

faq.ninos: It has a battery that runs on the heat of a radioactive material, inside a very tough capsule.
faq.org: Yes: SNAP-27 with ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 dioxide (NASA RPS); the ALSEP operated until 1977.

luna-apollo-14-lm-ascenso.nombre: Ascent stage of the lunar module Antares (Apollo 14)
luna-apollo-14-lm-ascenso.casi_fallo: Docking failed six times; a little ball of solder almost triggered the abort button.
luna-apollo-14-lm-ascenso.leccion: Anticipate how something can fail and prepare alternatives beforehand.
luna-apollo-14-lm-ascenso.logro: Deliberate impact recorded by two seismometers (Apollo 12 and 14): first measurement with a two-station network.
luna-apollo-14-lm-ascenso.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-14-lm-ascenso.nota: Coordinates estimated from seismic data (Toksoz et al. 1974; Orloff 2000; Wagner et al. 2017).

texto.ninos: This cabin was crashed on purpose 67 kilometres from where it had landed, like the distance between two neighbouring towns. Two seismometers felt the quake at the same time. Why is it useful to listen from two places?
texto.org: Ascent stage of LM-8 from AS-509, targeted impact on Feb 7, 1971 at 3.42 S, 19.67 W; coordinates estimated from seismic data (NSSDCA code 'm'). Recorded by the Apollo 12 and 14 PSEs. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Science: the blow helped us learn what the Moon is like inside.
faq.org: Controlled seismic source to calibrate the ALSEP seismometer network (LROC, impacts recorded by the Apollo seismic network).

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: It has not been found in photos yet; the place was calculated from the quake.
faq.org: Not identified by LROC; seismic position with an uncertainty of kilometres.

faq.pregunta: What almost went wrong on Apollo 14?
faq.ninos: The spacecraft would not latch on and a little ball of metal almost triggered the abort button.
faq.org: Six docking failures; ball of solder in the abort switch. Lesson: anticipate failure modes and prepare alternatives (Johnson, 2018).

luna-apollo-15-s-ivb.casi_fallo: A loose wire floating in zero gravity caused a short circuit; on the way back 1 of 3 parachutes failed.
luna-apollo-15-s-ivb.leccion: Flight produces failures that cannot be seen on Earth.
luna-apollo-15-s-ivb.logro: Impact recorded by the Apollo 12 and 14 seismometers; it helped measure the thickness of the lunar crust.
luna-apollo-15-s-ivb.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-15-s-ivb.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: Another 14-tonne rocket sent into the Moon on purpose, at more than 9,000 kilometres per hour, ten times faster than a plane. The seismometers felt it from hundreds of kilometres away. What would happen if you hit a very big ball with a marble?
texto.org: S-IVB from AS-510, impact on Jul 29, 1971 at 1.2897 S, 11.8245 W; site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Recorded by the Apollo 12 and 14 PSEs. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, as a new crater that shows up in the photos.
faq.org: Yes; crater identified by LROC.

faq.ninos: A floating wire caused a short circuit, and on the way back one of the three parachutes did not open.
faq.org: Short circuit from a loose wire in microgravity; at splashdown 1 of 3 main parachutes failed (Johnson, 2018).

faq.ninos: That things happen in space that cannot be seen on Earth.
faq.org: Flight produces failure modes that ground tests do not reproduce.

luna-apollo-15-lm-descenso.nombre: Descent stage of the lunar module Falcon (Apollo 15)
luna-apollo-15-lm-descenso.objeto: Lunar module descent stage (LM-10, Falcon), ALSEP, retroreflector and lunar roving vehicle (LRV-1)
luna-apollo-15-lm-descenso.casi_fallo: A loose wire floating in zero gravity caused a short circuit; on the way back 1 of 3 parachutes failed.
luna-apollo-15-lm-descenso.leccion: Flight produces failures that cannot be seen on Earth.
luna-apollo-15-lm-descenso.logro: First use of the lunar roving vehicle (LRV). It brought back 77.31 kg of samples, including the 'Genesis Rock'. Its 300-prism retroreflector is the most used today.
luna-apollo-15-lm-descenso.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-apollo-15-lm-descenso.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-apollo-15-lm-descenso.radiactivo_detalle: ALSEP SNAP-27, ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 oxide

texto.ninos: Here the astronauts drove the first car on the Moon and covered 28 kilometres, like going to school and back several times. They left the biggest laser mirror, which still answers from Earth. Where would you go in that car?
texto.org: Descent stage of LM-10 from AS-510, landing on Jul 30, 1971 at 26.13239 N, 3.63330 E (Hadley-Apennines); site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). 300-prism retroreflector active in the ILRS; ALSEP with SNAP-27. Sources: NSSDCA, ILRS, NASA RPS.

faq.ninos: Yes: the spacecraft, the car and the laser mirror, which is still working.
faq.org: Yes; stage, LRV-1, ALSEP and retroreflector visible in LROC; the retroreflector is the one most used by laser stations (ILRS).

faq.ninos: A loose wire caused a short circuit and one parachute did not open on the way back.
faq.org: Short circuit from a floating wire in microgravity; failure of 1 of 3 parachutes at splashdown (Johnson, 2018).

faq.ninos: It carries a well-protected radioactive heat battery to power the instruments.
faq.org: Yes: SNAP-27 with ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 dioxide (NASA RPS).

luna-apollo-15-lm-ascenso.nombre: Ascent stage of the lunar module Falcon (Apollo 15)
luna-apollo-15-lm-ascenso.casi_fallo: A loose wire floating in zero gravity caused a short circuit; on the way back 1 of 3 parachutes failed.
luna-apollo-15-lm-ascenso.leccion: Flight produces failures that cannot be seen on Earth.
luna-apollo-15-lm-ascenso.logro: Deliberate impact recorded by three seismometers (Apollo 12, 14 and 15).
luna-apollo-15-lm-ascenso.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-15-lm-ascenso.nota: Coordinates estimated from seismic data (Toksoz et al. 1974; Orloff 2000; Wagner et al. 2017).

texto.ninos: This cabin was crashed on purpose very close to where it had landed, about 90 kilometres away, like a short train ride. Three seismometers heard the blow. What would you say if the Moon could tell you what it felt?
texto.org: Ascent stage of LM-10 from AS-510, targeted impact on Aug 3, 1971 at 26.36 N, 0.25 E; coordinates estimated from seismic data (NSSDCA code 'm'). Recorded by the Apollo 12, 14 and 15 PSEs. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Science: every blow helped us learn about the inside of the Moon.
faq.org: Controlled seismic source for the ALSEP network (LROC, impacts recorded by the Apollo seismic network).

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: It has not been photographed yet; the place was calculated from the quake.
faq.org: Not identified by LROC; seismic position (Toksöz et al. 1974).

faq.pregunta: What almost went wrong on Apollo 15?
faq.ninos: A loose wire caused a short circuit, and one parachute failed on the way back.
faq.org: Short circuit from a floating wire; failure of 1 of 3 parachutes. Lesson: flight produces failures that cannot be seen on Earth (Johnson, 2018).

luna-luna-18.objeto: Sample-return probe that crashed during descent
luna-luna-18.casi_fallo: The signal cut out at the moment of landing on mountainous terrain; the probe crashed.
luna-luna-18.leccion: Rough terrain demands better descent sensors; its successor, Luna 20, landed very close by and did bring back samples.
luna-luna-18.logro: Its descent data helped Luna 20 accomplish the same task five months later.
luna-luna-18.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-luna-18.nota: Unconfirmed; contact lost ~100 m above the surface.

texto.ninos: This probe wanted to bring back lunar dust, but it crashed into some mountains and went silent forever. It weighed 5,600 kilos, like an elephant. Did you know that its sister Luna 20 succeeded in the same place soon afterwards?
texto.org: Luna 18, loss of signal while landing on Sep 11, 1971 at 3.76 N, 56.66 E (mountainous area next to Mare Fecunditatis). Unconfirmed site: an object in LROC images could be the lander (NSSDCA code 'n'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Its pieces are surely there, but nobody is completely sure which speck in the photos is the probe.
faq.org: Probably. LROC identified a candidate object at the estimated coordinates, but the identification is not confirmed (code 'n').

faq.ninos: It taught that landing among mountains is very hard, and so the next probe did succeed.
faq.org: It is a case of failure with a direct lesson: Luna 20 landed a few kilometres away in Feb 1972 and returned highland samples.

luna-luna-20.objeto: Descent stage of the sample-return probe
luna-luna-20.casi_fallo: It landed in the same mountainous area where Luna 18 had crashed five months earlier.
luna-luna-20.leccion: Repeating the attempt with what was learned turns a failure into a success.
luna-luna-20.logro: It brought back about 55 grams of soil from the lunar highlands, different from that of the maria.
luna-luna-20.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-luna-20.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This robot landed right where another one had crashed and brought back 55 grams of lunar soil, like a handful of sand. It came from the mountains of the Moon, a place nobody had touched. What colour do you think that sand was?
texto.org: Luna 20 descent stage, landing on Feb 21, 1972 at 3.7863 N, 56.6242 E (Apollonius highlands); the ascent stage returned ~55 g of regolith. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, the base of the robot stayed in the mountains and can be seen in photos taken from orbit.
faq.org: Yes. The descent stage remains at the site and was identified by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd').

faq.ninos: It brought back sand from the lunar mountains, which is different from that of the dark seas.
faq.org: First sample return from anorthositic highlands; it complemented the Luna 16 basalts and allowed comparison with Apollo 16.

luna-apollo-16-s-ivb.casi_fallo: The mass spectrometer boom did not retract and had to be jettisoned. The ascent stage lost control and could not be steered.
luna-apollo-16-s-ivb.leccion: Plans must include what to do when a tool cannot be stowed.
luna-apollo-16-s-ivb.logro: Impact recorded by the seismic network; the exact site was lost for years because of a tracking failure and LROC found it in 2015.
luna-apollo-16-s-ivb.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-16-s-ivb.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This rocket was crashed on purpose, but the signal was lost and for 43 years nobody knew exactly where it fell. A camera in orbit found its 40-metre crater, the size of an Olympic pool. How would you look for one crater among millions?
texto.org: S-IVB from AS-511, impact on Apr 19, 1972 at 1.9210 N, 24.6230 W; tracking was lost before impact and the crater was identified by LROC in 2015 (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, its crater was found in photos in 2015.
faq.org: Yes; crater identified by LROC in 2015 after decades of ~30 km uncertainty.

faq.ninos: A boom carrying an instrument would not stow and had to be let go; the ascent cabin was left out of control.
faq.org: The mass spectrometer boom did not retract and was jettisoned; the ascent stage lost control and could not be steered to its impact (Johnson, 2018).

faq.ninos: The sources we reviewed do not say; it is an open question.
faq.org: No information in the sources reviewed.

luna-apollo-16-lm-descenso.nombre: Descent stage of the lunar module Orion (Apollo 16)
luna-apollo-16-lm-descenso.objeto: Lunar module descent stage (LM-11, Orion), ALSEP and lunar roving vehicle (LRV-2)
luna-apollo-16-lm-descenso.casi_fallo: The mass spectrometer boom did not retract and had to be jettisoned. The ascent stage lost control and could not be steered.
luna-apollo-16-lm-descenso.leccion: Plans must include what to do when a tool cannot be stowed.
luna-apollo-16-lm-descenso.logro: The only landing in the highlands (Descartes). It brought back 95.71 kg of samples and operated the first ultraviolet telescope on another world.
luna-apollo-16-lm-descenso.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-apollo-16-lm-descenso.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-apollo-16-lm-descenso.radiactivo_detalle: ALSEP SNAP-27, ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 oxide

texto.ninos: This is where the only mission that went down to the Moon's mountains landed. They brought back almost 96 kilos of rocks, like a large adult, and used the first telescope on another world. What would you see with a telescope from the Moon?
texto.org: Descent stage of LM-11 from AS-511, landing on Apr 21, 1972 at 8.9734 S, 15.5011 E (Descartes); site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). ALSEP with SNAP-27; LRV-2 and far-UV camera at the site. Sources: NSSDCA, NASA RPS.

faq.ninos: Yes, with the lunar car and the instruments.
faq.org: Yes; stage, LRV-2 and ALSEP visible in LROC. Site protected by the One Small Step Act.

faq.ninos: A boom carrying an instrument would not stow and they had to let it go.
faq.org: The CSM mass spectrometer boom did not retract and was jettisoned; the ascent stage lost control after separation (Johnson, 2018).

faq.ninos: It has a protected radioactive heat battery, for the instruments.
faq.org: Yes: SNAP-27 with ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 dioxide (NASA RPS).

luna-apollo-16-subsatelite.casi_fallo: The mass spectrometer boom did not retract and had to be jettisoned. The ascent stage lost control and could not be steered.
luna-apollo-16-subsatelite.leccion: Plans must include what to do when a tool cannot be stowed.
luna-apollo-16-subsatelite.logro: It fell in just 35 days: it showed that the Moon's uneven gravity (mascons) makes low orbits unstable.
luna-apollo-16-subsatelite.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-16-subsatelite.nota: Coordinates according to Ulivi and Harland (2004).

texto.ninos: This small satellite was meant to last a year, but the Moon has areas that pull harder and it brought it down in 35 days, a month and a few days. That is how we learned the Moon is 'lumpy' inside. Where would you put a satellite so it does not fall?
texto.org: Subsatellite PFS-2 (1972-031D) released on Apr 24, 1972 from the CSM of AS-511; the orbit-raising manoeuvre was skipped and decay caused by mascons made it hit on May 29, 1972 at 10.16 N, 111.9 E (NSSDCA code 'o', Ulivi and Harland 2004). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it fell on the far side of the Moon.
faq.org: It hit the far side; position from the literature, not confirmed by LROC.

faq.pregunta: Why did it fall so fast?
faq.ninos: Because the Moon has areas with more gravity that kept tugging at it.
faq.org: Mascons perturb low orbits; the raising manoeuvre was cancelled because of the CSM engine problem.

faq.pregunta: What almost went wrong on Apollo 16?
faq.ninos: A boom carrying an instrument would not stow and the ascent cabin lost control.
faq.org: Mass spectrometer boom not retracted and loss of control of the ascent stage (Johnson, 2018).

luna-apollo-17-s-ivb.casi_fallo: No serious failure in the sources reviewed. It was the last crewed mission to the Moon.
luna-apollo-17-s-ivb.logro: Last S-IVB impact; recorded by all four Apollo seismometers, it completed the 'sound map' of the lunar interior.
luna-apollo-17-s-ivb.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-17-s-ivb.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: Apollo's last giant rocket was also crashed on purpose. Four seismometers in different places felt the blow, like four ears listening to the same drum. What does a sound tell us about what is inside?
texto.org: S-IVB from AS-512, impact on Dec 10, 1972 at 4.1681 S, 12.3307 W; site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Recorded by the Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16 PSEs. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, as a crater that shows up in photos from orbit.
faq.org: Yes; crater identified by LROC.

faq.ninos: Nothing serious, from what we reviewed. It was the last mission with people on the Moon.
faq.org: No serious failure in the sources reviewed. Last crewed mission to the Moon.

faq.ninos: To make a known quake and listen to how it travels through the inside of the Moon.
faq.org: Seismic source of known mass and velocity to calibrate the ALSEP network and estimate the structure of the crust.

luna-apollo-17-lm-descenso.nombre: Descent stage of the lunar module Challenger (Apollo 17)
luna-apollo-17-lm-descenso.objeto: Lunar module descent stage (LM-12, Challenger), ALSEP and lunar roving vehicle (LRV-3)
luna-apollo-17-lm-descenso.casi_fallo: No serious failure in the sources reviewed. It was the last crewed mission to the Moon.
luna-apollo-17-lm-descenso.logro: Last human footprint on the Moon (Dec 14, 1972). It brought back 110.52 kg of samples, the record, with the first geologist astronaut.
luna-apollo-17-lm-descenso.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-apollo-17-lm-descenso.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-apollo-17-lm-descenso.radiactivo_detalle: ALSEP SNAP-27, ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 oxide

texto.ninos: This is where the last human footprints on the Moon were left, in 1972. They brought back 110 kilos of rocks, like two adults together, and a geologist found orange soil. When do you think someone will step on this place again?
texto.org: Descent stage of LM-12 from AS-512, landing on Dec 11, 1972 at 20.1911 N, 30.7723 E (Taurus-Littrow); site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). ALSEP with SNAP-27; LRV-3 at the site. Sources: NSSDCA, NASA RPS.

faq.ninos: Yes, with the lunar car and the astronauts' footprints.
faq.org: Yes; stage, LRV-3, ALSEP and footprints visible in LROC. Site protected by the One Small Step Act.

faq.ninos: Nothing serious, from what we reviewed. It was the last mission with people.
faq.org: No serious failure in the sources reviewed; close of the crewed programme.

faq.ninos: It has a protected radioactive heat battery, for the instruments.
faq.org: Yes: SNAP-27 with ~3.9 kg of Pu-238 dioxide (NASA RPS); the ALSEP worked until 1977.

luna-apollo-17-lm-ascenso.nombre: Ascent stage of the lunar module Challenger (Apollo 17)
luna-apollo-17-lm-ascenso.casi_fallo: No serious failure in the sources reviewed. It was the last crewed mission to the Moon.
luna-apollo-17-lm-ascenso.logro: Last deliberate impact of the Apollo programme, recorded by the network of four seismometers.
luna-apollo-17-lm-ascenso.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-apollo-17-lm-ascenso.nota: Coordinates estimated from seismic data (Toksoz et al. 1974; Orloff 2000; Wagner et al. 2017).

texto.ninos: Apollo's last cabin was also crashed on purpose, about 10 kilometres from where it landed, like going from one end of a city to the other. It was the last blow the Apollo seismometers heard. What would you have left on the Moon?
texto.org: Ascent stage of LM-12 from AS-512, targeted impact on Dec 15, 1972 at 19.97 N, 30.49 E; coordinates estimated from seismic data (NSSDCA code 'm'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Science: the blow was used to listen to the inside of the Moon.
faq.org: Controlled seismic source recorded by the Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16 PSEs.

faq.pregunta: Can it be seen from orbit?
faq.ninos: It has not been photographed yet; the place was calculated from the quake.
faq.org: Not identified by LROC; seismic position (Toksöz et al. 1974).

faq.pregunta: What almost went wrong on Apollo 17?
faq.ninos: Nothing serious, from what we reviewed.
faq.org: No serious failure in the sources reviewed; last crewed mission to the Moon.

luna-apollo-16-lm-ascenso.nombre: Ascent stage of the lunar module Orion (Apollo 16)
luna-apollo-16-lm-ascenso.casi_fallo: The mass spectrometer boom did not retract and had to be jettisoned. The ascent stage lost control and could not be steered.
luna-apollo-16-lm-ascenso.leccion: Plans must include what to do when a tool cannot be stowed.
luna-apollo-16-lm-ascenso.logro: It was meant to crash as a seismic source, but it lost control; it fell by itself months later at an unknown site.
luna-apollo-16-lm-ascenso.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-apollo-16-lm-ascenso.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: This cabin was going to be crashed on purpose to make a quake, but it started tumbling out of control. It spent almost a year circling the Moon, more than 4,000 laps, and fell where nobody knows. What would you do if your spacecraft did not obey?
texto.org: Ascent stage of LM-11 from AS-511; after separation it lost attitude control and the targeted impact could not be carried out. The orbit decayed between 1972 and 1973; site unknown (NSSDCA code 'g'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: It fell on the Moon, but nobody knows where.
faq.org: Impact not located after orbital decay; not identified by LROC.

faq.ninos: It lost control on separation and could not be steered.
faq.org: Loss of attitude control after separation; the impact planned as a seismic source did not take place (Johnson, 2018).

faq.ninos: The sources we reviewed do not say.
faq.org: No information in the sources reviewed.

luna-apollo-16-brazo-espectrometro.objeto: Extendable boom of the service module mass spectrometer
luna-apollo-16-brazo-espectrometro.casi_fallo: The mass spectrometer boom did not retract and had to be jettisoned. The ascent stage lost control and could not be steered.
luna-apollo-16-brazo-espectrometro.leccion: Plans must include what to do when a tool cannot be stowed.
luna-apollo-16-brazo-espectrometro.logro: An example of a loose part: an instrument boom that could not be stowed and was left in lunar orbit.
luna-apollo-16-brazo-espectrometro.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-apollo-16-brazo-espectrometro.nota: Apollo 16 mass spectrometer boom, jettisoned because it did not retract.

texto.ninos: A long boom carrying an instrument got stuck and would not stow, so they let it go in orbit. It was about 7 metres long, like two cars in a row, and nobody knows where it fell. What would you do with something that does not fit in your backpack?
texto.org: Mass spectrometer boom from the SIM bay of the AS-511 CSM, jettisoned in lunar orbit in April 1972 after retraction failed (NSSDCA code 'p'); impact site unknown. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: It fell somewhere on the Moon that nobody knows.
faq.org: Impact not located; not identified by LROC.

faq.ninos: Because with the boom sticking out they could not fire the engine to come home.
faq.org: Retraction failed and the extended boom put the trans-Earth injection burn at risk.

faq.ninos: The sources we reviewed do not say.
faq.org: No information in the sources reviewed.

luna-luna-21.objeto: Landing platform with ramps for the Lunokhod 2 rover
luna-luna-21.leccion: A design that has already worked (Luna 17) can be repeated with improvements instead of starting from scratch.
luna-luna-21.logro: It took the Lunokhod 2 rover to Le Monnier crater, just 180 kilometres from the Apollo 17 site.
luna-luna-21.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-luna-21.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This platform lowered a second lunar car just 180 kilometres from where the last astronauts had walked, like from one city to the next. Do you think the little car saw their footprints?
