texto.org: Luna 21 landing platform, landing on Jan 15, 1973 at 25.9994 N, 30.4076 E (Le Monnier crater); it deployed the Lunokhod 2 rover. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, the platform is still on the edge of a crater, motionless since 1973.
faq.org: Yes. It remains in Le Monnier and was identified in LROC images (NSSDCA code 'd').

faq.ninos: It was the Soviet Union's last lunar garage and it delivered the little car that travelled the furthest.
faq.org: Last Soviet rover platform; its position anchors the traverse of Lunokhod 2, used as a reference for distances on the surface.

luna-lunokhod-2.objeto: Eight-wheeled exploration vehicle with a laser retroreflector
luna-lunokhod-2.casi_fallo: When it brushed against a crater wall, the open lid scooped up dust; when the lid was closed, the dust fell onto the radiator and the rover overheated.
luna-lunokhod-2.leccion: Lunar dust is a real enemy: you have to design so it never touches radiators or panels.
luna-lunokhod-2.logro: It travelled about 39 kilometres in four months, the record beyond Earth until 2014; its retroreflector is still in use.
luna-lunokhod-2.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-lunokhod-2.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-lunokhod-2.radiactivo_detalle: Polonium-210 heater to survive the lunar night

texto.ninos: This little car travelled 39 kilometres on the Moon, almost a marathon, and nobody beat it for 41 years. A little dust made it overheat and it shut down, but its mirror still bounces back laser beams. What would you protect from the dust?
texto.org: Lunokhod 2 rover (Luna 21), operated from Jan 15, 1973 to May 11, 1973 at 25.8323 N, 30.9222 E; it travelled ~39 km, the off-Earth distance record until Opportunity surpassed it in 2014. Located by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'); its laser retroreflector is still used by the ILRS network. Source: NSSDCA, ILRS.

faq.ninos: Yes, it is stopped where it shut down, and its mirror still answers laser light from Earth.
faq.org: Yes. It remains in Le Monnier; LROC photographed it and its retroreflector receives laser measurements from ILRS stations.

faq.ninos: It travelled further than any other robot beyond Earth for 41 years and it still helps measure the distance to the Moon.
faq.org: Surface distance record until 2014 and one of the five active lunar retroreflectors; its dust failure is a reference case in rover thermal design.

luna-luna-19.objeto: Heavy orbiter left in lunar orbit
luna-luna-19.leccion: Whatever is left in low lunar orbit ends up falling, and nobody knows where.
luna-luna-19.logro: It orbited the Moon for more than a year measuring its gravity field and the nearby radiation.
luna-luna-19.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-luna-19.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: This satellite circled the Moon for more than 1 year, like a clock that never stopped, and then fell somewhere nobody knows. Where do you think it is today?
texto.org: Luna 19 orbiter, in lunar orbit from Oct 3, 1971; the orbit decayed around 1973 and the impact site is unknown (NSSDCA code 'g'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: It is on the Moon, yes, but it fell without anyone seeing it and we do not know where.
faq.org: Yes, it hit the surface after orbital decay (estimated 1973), but there are no coordinates and no identification in LROC images.

faq.ninos: It is one of the Moon's lost objects: it reminds us that we do not know where everything we sent ended up.
faq.org: An example of the 18 objects in the NSSDCA catalogue with unknown whereabouts; its orbit data helped map the gravity anomalies (mascons).

luna-explorer-35.objeto: Science satellite left in lunar orbit
luna-explorer-35.leccion: A switched-off satellite in lunar orbit ends up falling without anyone seeing it.
luna-explorer-35.logro: It measured the solar wind and the magnetic field near the Moon for six years and showed that the Moon has no global magnetic field.
luna-explorer-35.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-explorer-35.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: This small satellite, 104 kilos like a fridge, circled the Moon for six years listening to the Sun's wind. When it was switched off, it fell somewhere nobody knows. What sound do you think the solar wind makes?
texto.org: Explorer 35 (IMP-E), in lunar orbit from Jul 1967; switched off on Jun 24, 1973, with later orbital decay and unknown impact site (NSSDCA code 'g'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but it fell with no witnesses: it is at some point on the Moon that nobody has found.
faq.org: Yes; the orbit decayed after 1973 and there are no impact coordinates and no identification in LROC images.

faq.ninos: It taught us that the Moon does not have a giant magnet inside like Earth does.
faq.org: It confirmed the absence of a global lunar magnetic field and characterised the interaction of the solar wind with the Moon; it is one of the NASA objects with unknown whereabouts.

luna-apollo-15-subsatelite.casi_fallo: A loose wire floating in zero gravity caused a short circuit; on the way back 1 of 3 parachutes failed.
luna-apollo-15-subsatelite.leccion: Flight produces failures that cannot be seen on Earth.
luna-apollo-15-subsatelite.logro: First satellite launched from a crewed spacecraft in lunar orbit; it measured the magnetic field and particles for more than a year.
luna-apollo-15-subsatelite.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-apollo-15-subsatelite.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: The astronauts released this small satellite, 36 kilos like a big dog, to circle the Moon measuring its magnetic field. In the end it fell and nobody knows where. How would you look for something so small on the Moon?
texto.org: Subsatellite PFS-1 (1971-063D) released on Aug 4, 1971 from the CSM of AS-510; the orbit decayed around 1973 and the impact site is unknown (NSSDCA code 'g'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: It fell on the Moon somewhere nobody knows.
faq.org: Decayed orbit with impact not located; not identified by LROC.

faq.ninos: To measure invisible things: the magnetism and the particles around the Moon.
faq.org: Magnetometer, particle detector and tracking of mass concentrations (mascons) through orbital variations.

faq.pregunta: What almost went wrong on Apollo 15?
faq.ninos: A loose wire caused a short circuit and one parachute failed on the way back.
faq.org: Short circuit in microgravity and failure of 1 of 3 parachutes; lesson: flight produces failures that cannot be seen on Earth (Johnson, 2018).

luna-luna-23.casi_fallo: It landed too hard and tipped over; the drill was damaged and could not take samples.
luna-luna-23.leccion: A rough landing can leave the equipment intact but useless; the descent speed has to be measured well.
luna-luna-23.logro: Its failure defined the site and design of Luna 24, which did bring back samples from the same place two years later.
luna-luna-23.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-luna-23.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This probe reached the Moon, but it fell on its side like a tortoise and its drill broke. It weighed 5,800 kilos, more than a lorry. What would you do if your robot fell on its side so far from home?
texto.org: Luna 23, hard landing on Nov 6, 1974 at 12.6667 N, 62.1511 E (Mare Crisium); the drilling system was left inoperative and there was no sample return. LROC shows the spacecraft tipped over (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it is still lying on its side in the Sea of Crises and can be seen in photos from orbit.
faq.org: Yes. LROC identified the tipped-over probe in Mare Crisium (NSSDCA code 'd'), about 2 km from the Luna 24 site.

faq.ninos: Its fall taught how to land better, and its sister Luna 24 did bring back sand from the Moon.
faq.org: A case of landing with structural damage; its telemetry guided Luna 24 (Aug 1976), which returned 170 g from the same mare.

luna-luna-24.objeto: Descent stage of the sample-return probe
luna-luna-24.casi_fallo: It landed about 2 kilometres from where Luna 23 had tipped over two years earlier.
luna-luna-24.leccion: Going back to the same site with what was learned turns a failure into the successful close of a programme.
luna-luna-24.logro: It brought back 170 grams of soil from up to 2 metres deep; traces of water were found in it. It was the last Soviet mission to the Moon.
luna-luna-24.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-luna-24.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This was the last Soviet robot on the Moon and it brought back 170 grams of soil, like an apple. Inside that soil they found a tiny bit of water. Did you think the Moon was completely dry?
texto.org: Luna 24 descent stage, landing on Aug 18, 1976 at 12.7142 N, 62.2129 E (Mare Crisium); the ascent stage returned 170 g from a ~2 m core on Aug 22, 1976. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, the base of the robot is still in the Sea of Crises, near its tipped-over sister.
faq.org: Yes. The descent stage remains in Mare Crisium and has been identified by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd').

faq.ninos: It was the last visit by any country to the Moon for 37 years and it brought back hints of water.
faq.org: Last Moon landing before Chang'e 3 (2013); analysis of its samples reported ~0.1% water, a finding re-evaluated after the 2008-2009 discoveries.

luna-luna-22.objeto: Heavy orbiter left in lunar orbit
luna-luna-22.leccion: Without tracking until the end, the place where an orbiter falls is lost forever.
luna-luna-22.logro: It orbited the Moon for 18 months photographing the surface and measuring its gravity and the radiation.
luna-luna-22.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-luna-22.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: This satellite circled the Moon for 18 months, like a year and a half of school, taking photos. Then it ran out of fuel and fell somewhere nobody knows. Which photo would you have liked it to take?
texto.org: Luna 22 orbiter, in lunar orbit from Jun 2, 1974; it operated until Nov 1975, with orbital decay around 1976 and unknown impact site (NSSDCA code 'g'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it fell on the Moon, but nobody knows where.
faq.org: Yes; the orbit decayed after the end of the mission and there are no coordinates and no LROC identification.

faq.ninos: It is another of the lost objects: it shows that we need to write down where each thing falls.
faq.org: Last Soviet orbiter of the series; its gravimetric and photographic measurements supported the Luna 23 and 24 missions.

luna-explorer-49.objeto: Orbital radio telescope left in lunar orbit
luna-explorer-49.leccion: Using the Moon as a shield against Earth's radio noise works, but the device ends up falling unrecorded.
luna-explorer-49.logro: It listened to the universe in radio waves from behind the Moon, shielded from Earth's noise, with 229-metre antennas.
luna-explorer-49.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-explorer-49.nota: Left in lunar orbit untracked; its orbit decayed and it fell at an unknown site.

texto.ninos: This satellite unfolded 229-metre antennas, like two football pitches, to listen to space while hidden behind the Moon. Then it fell somewhere nobody knows. What would you listen to with those antennas?
texto.org: Explorer 49 (RAE-B), in lunar orbit from Jun 1973; end of operations in Aug 1977, with later orbital decay and unknown impact site (NSSDCA code 'g'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it fell on the Moon after 1977, but nobody knows where.
faq.org: Yes; the orbit decayed after 1977 and there are no coordinates and no LROC identification.

faq.ninos: It was the first radio telescope to use the Moon as a wall to block Earth's noise.
faq.org: Pioneer of low-frequency radio astronomy from the far side, a concept taken up again today by projects such as LuSEE-Night.

luna-hagoromo.objeto: Subsatellite released in lunar orbit with a failed transmitter
luna-hagoromo.casi_fallo: Its transmitter failed before reaching the Moon; only a telescope on Earth saw the engine burn that put it into lunar orbit.
luna-hagoromo.leccion: Without radio there is no tracking: a silent object becomes a lost object.
luna-hagoromo.logro: First Japanese satellite in lunar orbit (March 1990), although it could never tell us so.
luna-hagoromo.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.

texto.ninos: This satellite was tiny, 12 kilos like a medium-sized dog, and it went silent before arriving. Nobody knows whether it is still circling the Moon or has already fallen. Where would you look for it?
texto.org: Hagoromo subsatellite, released by Hiten on Mar 18, 1990 and inserted into lunar orbit with no telemetry; its decay or impact is unconfirmed and it may have moved into heliocentric orbit (NSSDCA code 'r'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Nobody knows: it may have fallen on the Moon or still be circling with nobody listening.
faq.org: Unknown. With no telemetry since 1990, there is no confirmation of impact or of it remaining in lunar orbit.

faq.ninos: It is the example of a truly lost object: we do not even know whether it is on the Moon.
faq.org: The only object in the catalogue whose presence on the Moon is uncertain; it illustrates the gap between what is launched and what is tracked.

luna-hiten.objeto: Navigation test probe crashed on purpose
luna-hiten.casi_fallo: Its subsatellite Hagoromo lost its transmitter; to enter lunar orbit a long, low-energy route that had never been tried before had to be used.
luna-hiten.leccion: When fuel is short, the gravity of the Sun and Earth can do the work if you are patient.
luna-hiten.logro: First Japanese lunar probe and the first to use a low-energy trajectory to be captured into lunar orbit.
luna-hiten.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.

texto.ninos: This probe reached the Moon by a very long, cheap route, letting gravity carry it, and in the end it was crashed on purpose. It weighed 143 kilos, like two adults. Would you take the long way if it saved you fuel?
texto.org: Hiten (MUSES-A), controlled impact on Apr 10, 1993 at 34.0 S, 55.3 E, estimated by Uesugi 1996 (NSSDCA code 'q'; alternative estimate 34.3 S, 55.6 E). First lunar capture via a low-energy ballistic trajectory. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, its remains are where it was crashed, although nobody has photographed the crater.
faq.org: Yes; the site is a trajectory estimate and has not been confirmed in LROC images.

faq.ninos: It was Japan's first probe at the Moon and it taught a new way of travelling on very little fuel.
faq.org: It demonstrated the Belbruno-Miller low-energy transfer, later used by SMART-1, GRAIL and CAPSTONE; Japan was the third country to reach the Moon.

luna-lunar-prospector.objeto: Orbiter crashed on purpose into a south-pole crater
luna-lunar-prospector.casi_fallo: The final impact aimed to raise a cloud of water vapour visible from Earth; nothing was detected.
luna-lunar-prospector.leccion: An experiment with no result also teaches: a bigger impact (LCROSS) was needed to confirm the ice.
luna-lunar-prospector.logro: It detected hydrogen at the lunar poles, the first strong hint of water ice; it carries the ashes of geologist Eugene Shoemaker.
luna-lunar-prospector.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-lunar-prospector.nota: Coordinates according to Ulivi and Harland (2004).

texto.ninos: This probe searched for frozen water on the Moon and in the end it was sent into a dark crater to see whether vapour would fly up. It carries the ashes of a scientist who dreamed of going to the Moon, 384,000 kilometres from his home. Would you like to rest so far away?
texto.org: Lunar Prospector, targeted impact on Jul 31, 1999 at 87.7 S, 42.0 E, a crater near the south pole (NSSDCA code 'o', source Ulivi and Harland 2004); no water plume was detected. It carried the ashes of Eugene Shoemaker. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, its pieces are in a crater near the Moon's south pole.
faq.org: Yes; the impact site is an estimate from the literature and has not been identified in LROC images.

faq.ninos: It was the first to say 'there may be ice here' at the Moon's poles.
faq.org: Its neutron spectrometer measured excess polar hydrogen, the basis for the LCROSS missions and for the Artemis search for resources.

luna-smart-1.leccion: A very weak but constant engine can take a spacecraft to the Moon on very little fuel.
luna-smart-1.logro: First European lunar mission and the first to reach the Moon with ion propulsion; its impact was observed from Earth.
luna-smart-1.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.

texto.ninos: This European spacecraft took 14 months to reach the Moon, longer than a school year, because its engine pushed as gently as a puff of breath. In the end it was crashed on purpose and the flash was seen from Earth. Is it worth going slowly if you use less?
texto.org: SMART-1, controlled impact on Sep 3, 2006 at 34.4 S, 46.2 W (Lacus Excellentiae), characterised by Burchell et al. 2015 (NSSDCA code 's'). First European demonstration of solar electric propulsion to the Moon. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it left a small elongated crater where it struck the Moon a glancing blow.
faq.org: Yes; the very oblique impact crater was identified in LROC images by Burchell et al. 2015 (code 's').

faq.ninos: It was Europe's first spacecraft at the Moon and it tested a new engine that uses very little fuel.
faq.org: It validated ion propulsion for interplanetary missions (later BepiColombo) and mapped the Moon in X-rays and infrared.

luna-chandrayaan-1-mip.objeto: Impact probe released by the orbiter
luna-chandrayaan-1-mip.leccion: A small object dropped on purpose can measure the Moon's thin atmosphere as it falls.
luna-chandrayaan-1-mip.logro: India's first object on the Moon; its sensors detected water in the thin lunar atmosphere during descent.
luna-chandrayaan-1-mip.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-chandrayaan-1-mip.nota: It hit Shackleton crater; exact coordinates unknown.

texto.ninos: This little 34-kilo box, like a ten-year-old child, was released from orbit and fell for 25 minutes until it hit near the south pole. As it fell, it sniffed a tiny bit of water. What would you measure during a fall like that?
texto.org: Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe, impact on Nov 14, 2008 in Shackleton crater, near the south pole (~89 S, 30 W; exact coordinates unknown, NSSDCA code 't'). Its CHACE mass spectrometer detected water during descent. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it crashed inside a very dark crater at the south pole and its remains are still there.
faq.org: Yes; it hit Shackleton, but the exact point is not known and has not been identified by LROC (code 't').

faq.ninos: It was the first thing from India to touch the Moon and it helped discover that there is water there.
faq.org: It made India the fourth country to reach the lunar surface and provided independent evidence of water, alongside M3 and Cassini.

luna-okina.leccion: To measure the gravity of the far side you need a messenger that can see both the spacecraft and Earth at once.
luna-okina.logro: It relayed Kaguya's signals from behind the Moon and enabled the first direct gravity map of the far side.
luna-okina.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.

texto.ninos: This 53-kilo satellite, like a big dog, was the messenger for its mother ship: it passed on her signals when she hid behind the Moon. In the end it fell on the far side. How would you send a message from behind the Moon?
texto.org: Okina (Rstar) subsatellite of Kaguya, impact through orbital decay on Feb 12, 2009 at 28.213 N, 159.033 W, far side, according to the JAXA status report of Feb 18, 2009 (NSSDCA code 'u'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it fell on the side of the Moon we never see from Earth.
faq.org: Yes; the site comes from the JAXA report and has not been identified in LROC images.

faq.ninos: Thanks to it, the hidden side of the Moon could be weighed for the first time.
faq.org: It made possible the four-way Doppler tracking of Kaguya, the origin of the first direct gravity map of the far side.

luna-change-1.objeto: Orbiter crashed on purpose at the end of its mission
luna-change-1.leccion: A controlled impact at the end of the mission avoids leaving an object adrift in orbit.
luna-change-1.logro: China's first lunar mission; it made a complete three-dimensional map of the Moon and measured the thickness of the soil with microwaves.
luna-change-1.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-change-1.nota: According to Xinhua (2009); Siddiqi (2018) gives other coordinates.

texto.ninos: This was China's first spacecraft at the Moon: it spent more than 1 year circling it and drawing a complete map, like putting together a giant jigsaw puzzle. In the end it was crashed on purpose. Which part of the map would you look at first?
texto.org: Chang'e 1 orbiter, controlled impact on Mar 1, 2009 at 1.50 S, 52.36 E (Mare Fecunditatis), according to Xinhua 2009 (NSSDCA code 'w'; alternative coordinates 1.66 S, 52.27 E in Siddiqi 2018). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, its remains are in the Sea of Fertility, near where Luna 16 landed.
faq.org: Yes; the site comes from Chinese sources and has not been confirmed in LROC images (code 'w').

faq.ninos: It opened the way for the Chinese robots that later landed on the Moon.
faq.org: It began the Chang'e programme, which later achieved the first landing on the far side (2019) and sample returns (2020, 2024).

luna-kaguya.objeto: Main orbiter crashed on purpose at the end of its mission
luna-kaguya.leccion: Ending a mission with a planned and observed impact turns the ending into one more experiment.
luna-kaguya.logro: It recorded Earthrise over the lunar horizon in high definition and produced the most detailed topographic map of its time.
luna-kaguya.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.

texto.ninos: This Japanese spacecraft filmed Earth rising behind the Moon as if it were a sunrise. It weighed 2,900 kilos, like a hippopotamus, and in the end it was crashed on purpose. What would your home look like from there?
texto.org: Kaguya (SELENE) orbiter, controlled impact on Jun 10, 2009 at 65.5 S, 80.4 E, near Gill crater, according to the 2009 JAXA press release (NSSDCA code 'x'); the flash was observed by telescopes on Earth. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, its remains are near the south of the Moon, where the crash was seen from Earth.
faq.org: Yes; the site comes from the JAXA press release and is not identified in LROC images (code 'x').

faq.ninos: Its videos of Earth rising over the Moon are among the most beautiful that exist.
faq.org: It was the most complete lunar mission since Apollo up to that time: 14 instruments, global laser altimetry and the first gravity map of the far side.

luna-lcross-centaur.objeto: Centaur upper stage used as a projectile
luna-lcross-centaur.casi_fallo: The dust cloud was fainter than expected and was barely seen from Earth; the useful data came from the shepherding spacecraft and from LRO.
luna-lcross-centaur.leccion: An experiment can 'fail' for the public and still deliver the discovery: you have to measure with instruments, not with your eyes.
luna-lcross-centaur.logro: Its crash raised a cloud of dust with water ice from a permanently shadowed crater: the direct confirmation of water on the Moon.
luna-lcross-centaur.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-lcross-centaur.nota: It hit the permanently shadowed crater Cabeus.

texto.ninos: This empty 2,305-kilo rocket, like a car, was sent on purpose into a dark crater at the south pole. The dust that flew up contained water ice, like a lunar fridge. What would you do with water on the Moon?
texto.org: LCROSS Centaur stage, impact on Oct 9, 2009 at 84.6796 S, 48.7093 W, permanently shadowed Cabeus crater (Marshall et al. 2012, NSSDCA code 'y'). The ejecta plume contained ~155 kg of water vapour. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it left a new crater in a place the Sun never reaches.
faq.org: Yes; the crater in Cabeus is in permanent shadow and has been characterised by LRO (Diviner, LAMP), although with no direct optical image.

faq.ninos: It showed that there really is ice on the Moon, hidden in the dark craters.
faq.org: First direct detection of water in a permanently shadowed polar crater (~5.6% by mass), the basis for Artemis resource planning.

luna-lcross.objeto: Observation spacecraft that followed the projectile and also hit
luna-lcross.casi_fallo: Weeks earlier, a sensor fault made the spacecraft burn half its fuel in one day; just enough was left for the mission.
luna-lcross.leccion: A small software error can empty a tank: you have to watch consumption and keep a margin.
luna-lcross.logro: It flew through the Centaur's dust cloud for four minutes measuring water and other compounds before crashing.
luna-lcross.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-lcross.nota: It hit the permanently shadowed crater Cabeus.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft followed the rocket and flew through the dust cloud for 4 minutes, the length of a song, sniffing for water. Then it crashed into the Moon too. What would you smell in that cloud?
texto.org: LCROSS shepherding spacecraft, impact on Oct 9, 2009 at 84.719 S, 49.61 W, Cabeus crater, about 4 min after the Centaur (Marshall et al. 2012, NSSDCA code 'y'); its spectrometers measured water, CO, H2S and other volatiles in the plume. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it crashed in the same dark crater as the rocket, very close to it.
faq.org: Yes; it hit Cabeus ~2 km from the Centaur crater, in permanent shadow, with no direct optical image.

faq.ninos: Its sensors were the ones that really saw the ice in the dust that flew up.
faq.org: Its nine instruments provided the in situ measurement of the plume; together with LRO, it confirmed water ice and volatiles in Cabeus.

luna-ouna.objeto: Radio interferometry subsatellite left in orbit
luna-ouna.leccion: A satellite left untracked at the end of its life ends up as an object with unknown whereabouts.
luna-ouna.logro: Together with Okina it served as a radio source to measure the lunar orbit and gravity precisely.
luna-ouna.por_que_termino: Its exact whereabouts are unknown; it was left untracked or was lost during the mission.
luna-ouna.nota: Projected to have impacted; location unknown.

texto.ninos: This 53-kilo twin satellite, like a big dog, helped measure the Moon with radio waves. It was left circling in 2009 and nobody knows where it fell. What name would you give a crater nobody has seen?
texto.org: Ouna (Vstar) subsatellite of Kaguya, released in 2007 and left in lunar orbit after the end of the mission in 2009; projected impact location unknown (NSSDCA code 'v'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: It has almost certainly fallen on the Moon by now, but nobody knows at which point.
faq.org: It probably impacted after orbital decay, but no date or coordinates are on record.

faq.ninos: It is one of the Moon's lost objects that helped measure it very precisely.
faq.org: Part of Kaguya's VLBI experiment for lunar geodesy; an example of an object with no post-mission tracking.

luna-grail-a.objeto: Twin gravimetry probe crashed on purpose
luna-grail-a.leccion: Crashing the spacecraft at a chosen, photographed site avoids leaving a lost object and provides an extra experiment.
luna-grail-a.logro: With its twin it measured lunar gravity with unprecedented precision and revealed that the crust is thinner and more porous than thought.
luna-grail-a.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-grail-a.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This probe and its twin flew together measuring how the Moon tugged at them, like two friends holding hands. In the end they were sent into a mountain near the north pole, 200 kilos each, like a motorbike. Why do you think they were crashed on purpose?
texto.org: GRAIL A (Ebb), controlled impact on Dec 17, 2012 at 75.6088 N, 26.5940 W, on a rise near Goldschmidt crater; crater photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it left a tiny crater that a camera in orbit photographed.
faq.org: Yes. The impact crater was identified by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd') within a few metres of the prediction.

faq.ninos: Thanks to it we know what the Moon is like inside without digging.
faq.org: The GRAIL gravity map is the highest-resolution one of any celestial body and revealed dikes and a crust with ~12% porosity.

luna-grail-b.objeto: Twin gravimetry probe crashed on purpose
luna-grail-b.leccion: A planned ending honours the mission: the site was named in memory of an astronaut.
luna-grail-b.logro: Together with Ebb it completed the gravity map of the Moon; its impact site is named after Sally Ride, the first American woman in space.
luna-grail-b.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-grail-b.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This probe hit the Moon 30 seconds after its twin, the length of a TV advert. The place where they fell is named after Sally Ride, the first woman from her country to fly in space. Who would you dedicate a place on the Moon to?
texto.org: GRAIL B (Flow), controlled impact on Dec 17, 2012 at 75.6508 N, 26.8341 W, about 30 s after Ebb; crater photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). The site was named in honour of Sally Ride. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, its crater is next to its twin's and shows up in photos from orbit.
faq.org: Yes. The crater was identified by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd') next to that of GRAIL A.

faq.ninos: It helped draw the most precise gravity map of the Moon and its site honours an astronaut.
faq.org: Close of the GRAIL mission; the MoonKAM camera, run by Sally Ride's programme, let students photograph the Moon.

luna-change-3.casi_fallo: The descent was autonomous: the spacecraft had to dodge rocks by itself in the last 100 metres, with no help from Earth.
luna-change-3.leccion: A robot that decides for itself where to set down can avoid dangers nobody can see from home.
luna-change-3.logro: First soft landing since 1976 and the first Chinese spacecraft on the surface of the Moon; it carried an ultraviolet telescope that observed the sky from the Moon.
luna-change-3.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-change-3.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-change-3.radiactivo_detalle: Radioisotope heaters (plutonium-238) for the lunar night

texto.ninos: After 37 years with nobody landing softly on the Moon, this Chinese spacecraft did it: longer than many parents have been alive. Why did so much time pass without visits?
texto.org: Chang'e 3 lander, landing on Dec 14, 2013 at 44.1214 N, 19.5117 W (Mare Imbrium). Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, sitting still on a plain of cold lava. It no longer talks to Earth.
faq.org: Yes. The lander remains in Mare Imbrium; its instruments operated for several years and the site is confirmed by LROC images.

faq.ninos: Because it showed that landing gently on the Moon was still possible, and it opened the door to new visits.
faq.org: First soft landing in 37 years and China's first; it revived robotic surface exploration and is considered historic heritage.

luna-yutu.casi_fallo: A fault in the control mechanism left it immobile after its second lunar night, with only about 114 metres travelled.
luna-yutu.leccion: The extreme cold of the lunar night punishes moving parts; they have to be tested at those temperatures before flying.
luna-yutu.logro: First rover on the Moon since Lunokhod 2 (1973); although it could not move, it kept transmitting data for more than two years.
luna-yutu.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-yutu.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-yutu.radiactivo_detalle: Radioisotope heaters (plutonium-238) for the lunar night

texto.ninos: This wheeled robot came to a stop after travelling just 114 metres, like one block in your neighbourhood, but it kept sending messages for two years. Is a robot that cannot move still useful?
texto.org: Yutu rover of Chang'e 3, deployed on Dec 14, 2013 at 44.1208 N, 19.5122 W. It was immobilised in January 2014 after travelling about 114 m; site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, a few metres from its mother ship. It no longer moves or transmits.
faq.org: Yes. It remains about 20 m from the lander; it stopped transmitting in 2016. Position confirmed by LROC.

faq.ninos: Because its radar looked under the Moon's ground and showed us ancient layers of lava.
faq.org: Its ground-penetrating radar revealed the stratigraphy of the regolith and of lava flows in Mare Imbrium, new information about lunar volcanic history.

luna-ladee.objeto: Orbiter crashed on purpose at the end of its mission
luna-ladee.casi_fallo: It flew so low, sometimes below 50 km, that any orbit error would have crashed it early.
luna-ladee.leccion: Ending a mission with a planned impact avoids leaving an uncontrolled spacecraft in orbit.
luna-ladee.logro: It measured the Moon's extremely thin atmosphere and its levitating dust, and tested laser communication with Earth at 622 megabits per second.
luna-ladee.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-ladee.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This probe studied the Moon's almost invisible air and was then crashed on purpose on the far side, at about 5,800 kilometres per hour, faster than a bullet. Why does science sometimes end with a crash?
texto.org: LADEE, controlled impact on Apr 18, 2014 at 11.8494 N, 93.2494 W, far side. Impact crater photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Little pieces and a small crater remain on the side of the Moon we never see.
faq.org: Only debris and a crater about 3 m wide, located by LROC near the rim of Sundman V crater.

faq.ninos: Because it told us what the Moon's very thin air is made of before new spacecraft change it.
faq.org: It characterised the lunar exosphere and exospheric dust before the increase in missions alters it; it also demonstrated lunar optical communication.

luna-change-4.casi_fallo: On the far side there is no direct signal to Earth: everything depended on a relay satellite, Queqiao, placed months earlier.
luna-change-4.leccion: To explore where nobody can hear you, you first have to build the communication bridge.
luna-change-4.logro: First landing on the far side of the Moon, in Von Kármán crater; it sprouted cotton seeds in a small greenhouse.
luna-change-4.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-change-4.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).
luna-change-4.radiactivo_detalle: Radioisotope heaters (plutonium-238) and a small radioisotope thermoelectric generator for the lunar night

texto.ninos: Nobody had gone down to the far side of the Moon until this spacecraft did. A cotton seed even sprouted there, 384,000 kilometres from home, like going ten times around Earth. How do you talk to a spacecraft that the Moon is hiding?
texto.org: Chang'e 4 lander, landing on Jan 3, 2019 at 45.4561 S, 177.5885 E, Von Kármán crater (far side). Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'); communication via the Queqiao relay satellite. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, inside a huge crater on the side we never see from Earth.
faq.org: Yes. It remains in Von Kármán; some of its instruments kept operating for several years. Position confirmed by LROC.

faq.ninos: Because it is the first time something from Earth set down on the far side of the Moon.
faq.org: First landing on the far side; it is considered historic heritage and opened access to the South Pole–Aitken basin, the oldest on the Moon.

luna-yutu-2.casi_fallo: Its sibling Yutu had frozen after two lunar nights; this rover had to survive two-week nights at below minus 170 degrees.
luna-yutu-2.leccion: What failed once gets redesigned: Yutu 2 far outlived its predecessor.
luna-yutu-2.logro: First rover on the far side and the longest-operating one on the Moon; its radar measured the subsurface layers of Von Kármán crater.
luna-yutu-2.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-yutu-2.nota: Yutu 2 was still mobile in January 2023; final coordinates to be determined.
luna-yutu-2.radiactivo_detalle: Radioisotope heaters (plutonium-238) for the lunar night

texto.ninos: This robot has been roaming the far side of the Moon for more than 6 years, longer than primary school lasts. And it is still working. How far will it get?
texto.org: Yutu 2 rover of Chang'e 4, deployed on Jan 3, 2019; the coordinates 45.46 S, 177.59 E are those of the landing site, the rover is still mobile and its final position is yet to be defined (NSSDCA code 'z'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, and it is still awake: it is the only robot on this map that still travels across the Moon.
faq.org: Yes, and it remains operational. The catalogue coordinates are those of the landing; the rover has moved more than 1.5 km since then.

faq.ninos: Because it is the robot that has lasted the longest working on the Moon.
faq.org: Longevity record for a lunar rover and the first in situ radar and spectrometer data from the far side.

luna-beresheet.casi_fallo: A gyroscope failed during descent; when the computer was restarted, the main engine shut down and there was no time to recover it.
luna-beresheet.leccion: A single sensor with no backup can cost the whole mission in the final minutes.
luna-beresheet.logro: First private spacecraft and Israel's first to reach the Moon; it carried a 'lunar library' with thousands of dehydrated tardigrades, whose survival of the crash is considered very unlikely.
luna-beresheet.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-beresheet.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This spacecraft carried thousands of sleeping water bears, tiny creatures smaller than a grain of sand, and crashed at more than 3,000 kilometres per hour. They almost certainly did not survive. Should we take living things to the Moon?
texto.org: Beresheet (SpaceIL), unplanned impact on Apr 11, 2019 at 32.5956 N, 19.3496 E (Mare Serenitatis) due to a gyroscope failure and main engine shutdown. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). It carried dehydrated tardigrades; laboratory tests indicate they do not survive impacts at that speed (Traspas and Burchell, 2021).

faq.ninos: Debris and a dark smudge remain where it crashed. Nobody has gone to check.
faq.org: Yes, as a debris field; LROC photographed the impact mark. The state of the payload has not been verified.

faq.ninos: Because it raised the question of whether taking living things to other worlds without asking permission is right.
faq.org: A reference case for planetary protection and the governance of private biological payloads; the survival of the tardigrades is an open hypothesis, not a fact.

luna-longjiang-2.objeto: Microsatellite crashed on purpose at the end of its mission
luna-longjiang-2.casi_fallo: Its twin satellite, Longjiang 1, was lost on the way to the Moon; this was the only one of the two that arrived.
luna-longjiang-2.leccion: Launching as a pair gives a second chance if one fails.
luna-longjiang-2.logro: First microsatellite to orbit the Moon independently; it took a famous photo of Earth and the far side, with help from radio amateurs around the world.
luna-longjiang-2.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-longjiang-2.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: A small satellite like a washing machine, 47 kilos, took a photo of Earth behind the Moon and was then crashed on purpose so as not to leave junk circling. Why might crashing be better than staying in orbit?
texto.org: Longjiang 2 (Harbin Institute of Technology), controlled impact on Jul 31, 2019 at 16.6956 N, 159.5170 E, far side. Crater located by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Just a tiny crater on the far side, the size of a room.
faq.org: Yes, as a crater of about 4 by 5 m identified by LROC on the far side.

faq.ninos: Because it showed that a small, cheap spacecraft can explore the Moon too.
faq.org: It demonstrated the feasibility of independent lunar microsatellites and of radio amateurs taking part in receiving data.

luna-vikram-chandrayaan-2.casi_fallo: About 2 km up, in the final braking phase, it lost control and veered off; contact was cut before it touched the ground.
luna-vikram-chandrayaan-2.leccion: The last stretch of the descent needs room to manoeuvre: four years later, Chandrayaan-3 did it.
luna-vikram-chandrayaan-2.logro: India's first attempt at the lunar surface; its orbiter is still working and its debris was found in LRO images with the help of an amateur.
luna-vikram-chandrayaan-2.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-vikram-chandrayaan-2.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: Just 2 kilometres above the ground, about the height of 6 Eiffel Towers, this spacecraft lost its way and crashed. But its sister succeeded four years later. What do you learn when something goes wrong?
texto.org: Vikram, the Chandrayaan-2 lander, unplanned impact on Sep 6, 2019 at 70.8810 S, 22.7840 E after losing control in the fine braking phase. Debris identified by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, in pieces scattered near the Moon's south pole.
faq.org: Yes. LROC identified the debris field as several fragments scattered around the impact point.

faq.ninos: Because from this crash India learned what it needed to land well in 2023.
faq.org: Its lessons on control and redundancy were applied directly to the design of Chandrayaan-3, which landed successfully in 2023.

luna-change-5.casi_fallo: It had only two lunar days of light to drill, collect samples and lift off before night fell.
luna-change-5.leccion: A mission on a tight clock is designed to succeed even if some task is left incomplete.
luna-change-5.logro: It brought back 1,731 grams of lunar soil, the first samples since 1976, from young volcanic terrain near Mons Rümker.
luna-change-5.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-change-5.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This spacecraft collected almost 2 kilos of lunar soil, about the weight of a big bottle of water, and sent it back to Earth. What secrets does a handful of Moon dust hold?
texto.org: Chang'e 5 lander, landing on Dec 1, 2020 at 43.0576 N, 51.9161 W (Oceanus Procellarum, near Mons Rümker). It returned 1,731 g of samples; site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, the base stayed on the Moon; only the part with the samples went up.
faq.org: Yes. The descent module remains at the site; the ascent module lifted off on Dec 3, 2020 with the samples.

faq.ninos: Because its samples showed that the Moon had active volcanoes later than was thought.
faq.org: The samples date volcanic activity to about 2 billion years ago, much younger than those of Apollo and Luna, and recalibrate the lunar chronology.

luna-change-5-ascenso.objeto: Ascent module crashed on purpose after delivering the samples
luna-change-5-ascenso.casi_fallo: It had to lift off from the Moon and dock with the orbiter by itself, with nobody on board: a manoeuvre that had never been done robotically.
luna-change-5-ascenso.leccion: After doing its job, an empty spacecraft is brought down on purpose so it does not get in the way in orbit.
luna-change-5-ascenso.logro: First robotic rendezvous and docking in lunar orbit; it delivered the samples and was then crashed in a controlled way.
luna-change-5-ascenso.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-change-5-ascenso.nota: Chang'e 5 ascent stage crashed on purpose; most likely site: Regiomontanus crater.

texto.ninos: This small rocket rose from the Moon with the samples, delivered them in orbit and was then dropped on purpose. Nobody knows the exact point on a Moon with 38 million square kilometres, like four times Europe. Where might it have fallen?
texto.org: Chang'e 5 ascent module, controlled impact on Dec 7, 2020 after the sample transfer; impact site unknown (NSSDCA code 'aa'), most likely location near Regiomontanus crater. Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, but nobody has found the exact place where it fell.
faq.org: Yes, as unlocated impact debris; NSSDCA classifies it as whereabouts unknown (code 'aa').

faq.ninos: Because it shows that even a spacecraft that did its job well can end up lost on the map.
faq.org: An example of deliberate final disposal and of an object with no confirmed coordinates, useful for the debate on an open lunar inventory.

luna-cohete-no-identificado-2022.casi_fallo: Nobody was controlling it: it was a rocket stage that drifted through space for years until gravity took it into the Moon.
luna-cohete-no-identificado-2022.leccion: Without a shared record of what is launched, even a whole rocket can end up ownerless.
luna-cohete-no-identificado-2022.logro: First known lunar impact of uncontrolled space debris; its double crater suggests an unexplained extra mass on the rocket.
luna-cohete-no-identificado-2022.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-cohete-no-identificado-2022.nota: Probably the Chang'e 5-T1 booster (Mar 4, 2022); LROC photographed a double crater.

texto.ninos: A nameless rocket hit the Moon and left two holes side by side about 29 metres across, like a basketball court. Nobody says it is theirs. Whose might it be?
texto.org: Object WE0913A, impact on Mar 4, 2022 at 5.226 N, 125.514 W, near Hertzsprung crater (far side); double crater about 29 m wide photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'bb'). Identified as the probable Chang'e 5-T1 stage with an unexplained additional mass (Campbell et al., 2023); China denies it.

faq.ninos: Nobody has admitted it. Scientists think it came from a Chinese rocket, but China says no.
faq.org: No official attribution. The spectral and orbital analysis by Campbell et al. (2023) points to the Chang'e 5-T1 upper stage; CNSA denies it.

faq.ninos: Because it is the first piece of space debris that fell on the Moon without anyone planning it.
faq.org: It is the first documented lunar impact of uncontrolled debris and shows the lack of a mandatory catalogue of objects in cislunar space.

luna-hakuto-r-m1.casi_fallo: As it passed over a crater rim, the software discarded the real altitude reading, believing it to be wrong; the spacecraft thought it was on the ground when it was still 5 km up and ran out of fuel.
luna-hakuto-r-m1.leccion: Software that distrusts its own sensor can be more wrong than the sensor.
luna-hakuto-r-m1.logro: First Japanese private attempt; it carried the small Rashid rover from the United Arab Emirates, the first Arab lunar mission.
luna-hakuto-r-m1.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-hakuto-r-m1.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This spacecraft thought it had reached the ground when it was still 5 kilometres up, higher than the tallest mountain in the Alps, and it fell with no fuel left. What happens if you trust the plan more than what you see?
texto.org: Hakuto-R M1 (ispace), unplanned impact on Apr 25, 2023 at 47.581 N, 44.094 E (Atlas crater) due to an altitude estimation error and propellant depletion. Debris field photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, in pieces inside a crater called Atlas.
faq.org: Yes. LROC identified at least four fragments and changes in the regolith around the impact point.

faq.ninos: Because it was carrying the first Arab robot to the Moon and showed that companies are trying too.
faq.org: First Japanese commercial attempt and first lunar payload from the United Arab Emirates (Rashid rover); its failure analysis was applied to Mission 2.

luna-luna-25.casi_fallo: The engine burned for 127 seconds instead of 84 while lowering the orbit; the spacecraft lost too much altitude and crashed.
luna-luna-25.leccion: An engine burn cut off wrongly, even by seconds, turns an orbit into a crash.
luna-luna-25.logro: First Russian mission to the Moon since 1976; its crater about 10 metres wide was found by LRO a few days later.
luna-luna-25.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-luna-25.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: Its engine ran 43 seconds too long, less than the time it takes to brush your teeth, and that was enough to bring it down. How much can such a small mistake change?
texto.org: Luna 25 (Roscosmos), unplanned impact on Aug 19, 2023 at 57.865 S, 61.360 E after a braking burn longer than planned. New crater about 10 m wide photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, it left a new hole the size of a house near the south pole.
faq.org: Yes, as an impact crater about 10 m in diameter on the rim of Pontécoulant G crater, confirmed by LROC.

faq.ninos: Because Russia was returning to the Moon after 47 years and the trip ended in a crash.
faq.org: First Russian attempt after Luna 24 (1976); evidence that historical experience does not replace testing of current systems.

luna-chandrayaan-3.casi_fallo: Four years earlier, Chandrayaan-2's Vikram had crashed in the same area; this time it carried more fuel, stronger legs and a wider landing zone.
luna-chandrayaan-3.leccion: Studying the previous failure and fixing each cause turns a crash into a success.
luna-chandrayaan-3.logro: First landing near the lunar south pole and fourth country to land softly; it measured the soil temperature and detected sulphur in the regolith.
luna-chandrayaan-3.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-chandrayaan-3.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: India became the fourth country to land softly on the Moon, and it did so near the south pole, where the ground 8 centimetres down is as cold as a freezer. What might be hidden in the coldest places on the Moon?
texto.org: Vikram and Pragyan (Chandrayaan-3), landing on Aug 23, 2023 at 69.3741 S, 32.32 E, the highest latitude reached by a soft landing. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, the spacecraft and its little robot went to sleep when the lunar night came and never woke up again.
faq.org: Yes. Lander and rover entered hibernation mode in September 2023 and did not resume contact; they remain at the site.

faq.ninos: Because nobody had gone down so close to the south pole, where there could be ice.
faq.org: First in situ measurements of regolith temperature and composition at high southern latitude, the target area for future Artemis missions.

luna-slim.casi_fallo: At 50 metres above the ground the nozzle of one of its two engines came off; the spacecraft landed, but ended up upside down, with its solar panels facing the wrong way.
luna-slim.leccion: Setting down on the exact spot is not much use if the spacecraft ends up facing the ground; orientation matters as much as location.
luna-slim.logro: The most precise Moon landing in history, about 55 metres from the planned point, compared with the usual margin of kilometres.
luna-slim.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-slim.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This spacecraft arrived just 55 metres from where it wanted, like hitting a football pitch from the Moon, but it ended up upside down. Can something be a success and a stumble at the same time?
texto.org: SLIM (JAXA), landing on Jan 19, 2024 at 13.3160 S, 25.2510 E (near Shioli crater) with an accuracy of about 55 m; it ended up inverted after losing a nozzle. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, upside down next to a crater. It survived three lunar nights before going silent.
faq.org: Yes. It remains inverted at the site; it re-established contact after three lunar nights and the mission closed in August 2024.

faq.ninos: Because it showed that you can arrive right at the chosen place, not just 'somewhere nearby'.
faq.org: It validated crater-recognition navigation for precision landings, key for future high-value science sites.

luna-im-1-odysseus.casi_fallo: Its altitude lasers did not work because a safety switch was not removed before launch; an experimental NASA instrument served as a last-minute replacement, but the spacecraft came down fast and ended up on its side.
luna-im-1-odysseus.leccion: A backup instrument on board can save the mission when the main one fails.
luna-im-1-odysseus.logro: First US Moon landing since Apollo 17 (1972) and the first commercial spacecraft to land on the Moon.
luna-im-1-odysseus.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-im-1-odysseus.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: After 52 years with no American spacecraft on the Moon, more than half a century, this one arrived near the south pole, although it lay down on its side like a fallen skate. Does a landing count if you end up lying down?
texto.org: Odysseus (Nova-C, Intuitive Machines' IM-1 mission under NASA's CLPS programme), landing on Feb 22, 2024 at 80.13 S, 1.44 E near Malapert A crater; it ended up tilted on one side. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, lying on its side near the south pole; it worked for about seven days.
faq.org: Yes. It operated for about 7 days until the lunar night; it did not reactivate. Position confirmed by LROC.

faq.ninos: Because it was the first company, not a government, to land a spacecraft on the Moon.
faq.org: First commercial Moon landing and first American return to the surface in 52 years; it validated NASA's commercial payload model (CLPS).

luna-change-6.casi_fallo: All the work happened on the far side, where every command and every piece of data went through a relay satellite; without it, the spacecraft was alone.
luna-change-6.leccion: Repeating what worked (Chang'e 4 and 5) and combining it makes it possible to take a step nobody had taken.
luna-change-6.logro: First samples from the far side of the Moon: 1,935 grams from Apollo basin, inside the huge South Pole–Aitken basin.
luna-change-6.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-change-6.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This spacecraft brought back almost 2 kilos of rocks from the far side of the Moon, about the weight of a small cat, and nobody had done that before. Might they be different from the rocks on the side we see?
texto.org: Chang'e 6 lander, landing on Jun 1, 2024 at 41.6385 S, 153.9852 W (Apollo basin, far side). It returned 1,935 g of samples; site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, the base stayed on the far side; only the part with the samples lifted off.
faq.org: Yes. The descent module remains in Apollo basin; the ascent module lifted off on Jun 4, 2024.

faq.ninos: Because for the first time we can study rocks from the face we never see.
faq.org: First far-side sample; it allows the crust of both hemispheres and the history of the South Pole–Aitken basin to be compared.

luna-blue-ghost-1.casi_fallo: The two previous commercial spacecraft had ended up on their side or crashed; this one had to show that a commercial landing could go completely right.
luna-blue-ghost-1.leccion: Learning from other people's stumbles counts too: the third company to try did it upright and complete.
luna-blue-ghost-1.logro: First fully successful commercial Moon landing; it operated 10 NASA instruments for a full lunar day and filmed an eclipse from the Moon.
luna-blue-ghost-1.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-blue-ghost-1.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This spacecraft worked 14 days in a row on the Moon, a whole lunar day, like two weeks of holidays, and even recorded an eclipse. What must Earth look like covering the Sun?
texto.org: Blue Ghost 1 (Firefly Aerospace, NASA's CLPS programme), landing on Mar 2, 2025 at 18.562 N, 61.810 E (Mare Crisium). It operated for a full lunar day; site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, standing upright on a plain called the Sea of Crises.
faq.org: Yes. It remains upright in Mare Crisium; the mission ended when the lunar night arrived on Mar 16, 2025.

faq.ninos: Because it was the first landing by a company that went well from start to finish.
faq.org: First complete commercial success; its experiments included a thermal drill, a regolith collector and a navigation test with GPS/GNSS signals from the Moon.

luna-im-2-athena.casi_fallo: Like its predecessor, it ended up on its side inside a crater; with its panels badly oriented and the cold of the south pole, the mission lasted about a day.
luna-im-2-athena.leccion: A problem that repeats is not bad luck: the landing system needs to be redesigned.
luna-im-2-athena.logro: The closest landing to the south pole to date; it carried a drill and a spectrometer to look for water, which did not get to operate fully.
luna-im-2-athena.por_que_termino: It stayed on the lunar surface when its mission ended.
luna-im-2-athena.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This spacecraft came within 200 kilometres of the Moon's south pole, closer than anyone, but it fell on its side and shut down in 1 day. Why might it be so hard to stay upright on the Moon?
texto.org: Athena (Nova-C, Intuitive Machines' IM-2 mission under CLPS), landing on Mar 6, 2025 at 84.7906 S, 29.1957 E, the highest latitude of any Moon landing; it ended up on its side and the mission ended the next day. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, on its side inside a crater, very close to the south pole.
faq.org: Yes. It remains tilted in a crater near Mons Mouton; mission declared over on Mar 7, 2025.

faq.ninos: Because it set out to look for water in the coldest place we have touched on the Moon.
faq.org: The highest-latitude site reached by a spacecraft; it carried the PRIME-1 drill and a NASA mass spectrometer to detect volatiles.

luna-hakuto-r-m2.objeto: Crashed private lander, with the Tenacious micro-rover
luna-hakuto-r-m2.casi_fallo: The laser rangefinder delivered its data late; the spacecraft did not brake in time and touched the ground too fast.
luna-hakuto-r-m2.leccion: Fixing the cause of the first failure is not enough if another one appears in the same critical stretch: the final descent demands redundant sensors.
luna-hakuto-r-m2.logro: Second Japanese private attempt; it carried the Tenacious micro-rover, from Luxembourg, and a small red art house.
luna-hakuto-r-m2.por_que_termino: It hit the lunar surface at the end of its mission.
luna-hakuto-r-m2.nota: Object or crater photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera (LROC).

texto.ninos: This spacecraft carried a tiny 5-kilo robot, like a cat, and a little red toy house, but it reached the ground too fast and broke. Will they try a third time?
texto.org: Resilience (Hakuto-R M2, ispace), unplanned impact on Jun 5, 2025 at 60.4445 N, 4.588 W (Mare Frigoris) due to delayed laser rangefinder data and too fast a descent. Site photographed by LROC (NSSDCA code 'd'). Source: NSSDCA.

faq.ninos: Yes, in pieces on a cold plain in the north of the Moon, together with its little robot.
faq.org: Yes, as a debris field in Mare Frigoris; LROC recorded the impact mark. The Tenacious micro-rover was never deployed.

faq.ninos: Because it shows that reaching the Moon is still hard, even when you have tried before.
faq.org: Second consecutive failure by the same company in the descent phase; it reinforces the evidence that final braking is the highest-risk stretch of commercial missions.

marte-mars-2.casi_fallo: It entered the atmosphere at too steep an angle; the parachute did not deploy and it crashed.
marte-mars-2.leccion: Atmospheric entry needs a precise angle: a few degrees too many and the spacecraft has no time to brake.
marte-mars-2.logro: First human-made object to touch the surface of Mars, even if violently.
marte-mars-2.por_que_termino: It crashed during descent or landing.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft reached Mars before any other, but it arrived too fast and crashed. It weighed about as much as a small car, around 1,200 kilos. What do you think was left of it on the red ground?
texto.org: Mars 2 descent module (USSR), impact on Nov 27, 1971 at 45 S, 47 E (313 W) due to a failed entry profile; coordinates: Lakdawalla's map, The Planetary Society; status: Kilic 2022 (crashed spacecraft).

faq.ninos: Yes, but in pieces. Nobody has photographed it from orbit yet.
faq.org: The impact site has not been identified in orbital images; the position is the one estimated from the entry trajectory.

faq.ninos: It is history: it was the first thing humanity put on Mars, even though it broke.
faq.org: It is the first human artefact on the Martian surface; Kilic (2022) and Holcomb et al. (2024) propose treating these remains as an archaeological record.

marte-mars-3.objeto: Descent module (lander) with the PrOP-M mini-rover
marte-mars-3.casi_fallo: It landed in the middle of a global dust storm; it transmitted for about 20 seconds and shut down forever.
marte-mars-3.leccion: Getting there is not enough: you have to survive the local weather, and Mars has storms that cover the whole planet.
marte-mars-3.logro: First soft landing on Mars in history.
marte-mars-3.por_que_termino: It was left inactive on the Martian surface.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft was the first to land softly on Mars, but it only spoke for 20 seconds, less than the time it takes to tie your shoes. Then it went quiet. What might it have seen in those seconds?
texto.org: Mars 3 descent module (USSR), soft landing on Dec 2, 1971 at 45 S, 158 W; ~20 s transmission interrupted during the 1971 global dust storm. Coordinates: Lakdawalla's map, The Planetary Society; listed among the 9 inactive spacecraft by Kilic 2022.

faq.ninos: Yes. It has been sitting on a plain in the south of Mars for more than 50 years.
faq.org: Inactive since 1971. In 2013 candidate parachute, heat shield and lander were identified in MRO HiRISE images, without definitive confirmation.

faq.ninos: Nobody knows for certain. Perhaps the dust storm or a knock on landing.
faq.org: Cause undetermined; main hypotheses: damage on landing, electrical discharge from the dust storm or loss of the link with the orbiter.

marte-viking-1.casi_fallo: The original site looked too rocky in the orbiter's photos; another place had to be found and the landing delayed by several weeks.
marte-viking-1.leccion: Look carefully before going down: choosing the site with recent images saves the mission.
marte-viking-1.logro: First fully successful landing on Mars; it operated for more than 6 years and searched for life with three biological experiments.
marte-viking-1.por_que_termino: It was left inactive on the Martian surface.
marte-viking-1.nota: First successful US landing on Mars.
marte-viking-1.historia: The first American spacecraft to land successfully on Mars (Chryse Planitia) and transmit images from the surface.
marte-viking-1.legado_cientifico: It carried out the first in situ biological experiments looking for microbial metabolism, with ambiguous results attributed to soil chemistry.
marte-viking-1.equipo_dejado: Lander with a metal box body, dish antenna and mechanical arm with a sampling scoop.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft was the first to work well on Mars: it sent photos and looked for life for more than 6 years, as long as all of primary school. It ran on the heat of a special battery of radioactive material. What would you look for in the soil of Mars?
texto.org: Viking 1 Lander, landing on Jul 20, 1976 at 22.269 N, 47.951 W (Chryse Planitia), operational until Nov 1982; powered by two SNAP-19s with Pu-238. Coordinates: PDS Geosciences Node; status: Kilic 2022 (inactive).

faq.ninos: Yes, motionless and covered in dust. From orbit it looks like a tiny dot.
faq.org: Inactive since 1982 because of a command error that mispointed the antenna; the lander and its heat shield were photographed by MRO's HiRISE.

faq.ninos: It is sealed in very tough capsules and there is nobody nearby on Mars. It was its heat battery.
faq.org: The SNAP-19s use encapsulated Pu-238 as a heat source; the power decays with a half-life of 87.7 years. NASA RPS lists Viking among the missions with radioisotope generators.

marte-viking-2.casi_fallo: One leg ended up on a rock and the lander set down tilted by about 8 degrees; the orbiter also lost power during separation.
marte-viking-2.leccion: You have to design for the real terrain, not the ideal terrain.
marte-viking-2.logro: It photographed water frost on the Martian ground and operated until 1980 in Utopia Planitia.
marte-viking-2.por_que_termino: It was left inactive on the Martian surface.
marte-viking-2.historia: Twin of Viking 1, it landed in Utopia Planitia and transmitted images of a rocky landscape, including winter frost.
marte-viking-2.legado_cientifico: It complemented the biological and meteorological experiments of Viking 1 from a much higher latitude.
marte-viking-2.equipo_dejado: Lander with a metal box body, dish antenna and mechanical arm with a sampling scoop.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft landed a little crooked because one leg came down on a stone, but it worked for 4 years, like a faithful old dog. One morning it saw white frost on Mars. Can you imagine how cold it was?
texto.org: Viking 2 Lander, landing on Sep 3, 1976 at 47.668 N, 134.280 E (Utopia Planitia), operational until Apr 1980; powered by two SNAP-19s with Pu-238. Coordinates: PDS Geosciences Node; status: Kilic 2022 (inactive).

faq.ninos: Yes. It shut down when its batteries stopped working in 1980.
faq.org: Inactive since Apr 1980 due to battery failure; the lander has been identified in MRO HiRISE images.

faq.ninos: It saw thin ice on the ground, like the ice in a freezer. That shows there is water on Mars.
faq.org: It recorded seasonal water frost in Utopia Planitia and, together with Viking 1, obtained the first in situ analyses of Martian soil and atmosphere.

marte-pathfinder-sojourner.objeto: Lander (Carl Sagan Memorial Station) and Sojourner rover
marte-pathfinder-sojourner.estado: Inactive (communication was lost when the Pathfinder lander's battery ran down, September 1997)
marte-pathfinder-sojourner.casi_fallo: Nobody had landed with inflated airbags before; the spacecraft bounced more than 15 times before coming to rest.
marte-pathfinder-sojourner.leccion: Simple, cheap solutions can work: Pathfinder cost a fraction of Viking.
marte-pathfinder-sojourner.logro: First airbag landing and first rover on Mars: Sojourner, weighing 10.6 kg, travelled about 100 metres.
marte-pathfinder-sojourner.por_que_termino: It was left inactive on the Martian surface.
marte-pathfinder-sojourner.historia: The pioneer of all Mars rovers, delivered by the Pathfinder mission to Ares Vallis. It was the size of a microwave oven.
marte-pathfinder-sojourner.legado_cientifico: It showed that robotic vehicles could be operated on another planet and analysed the chemical composition of rocks with its X-ray spectrometer.
marte-pathfinder-sojourner.equipo_dejado: Small chassis, solar panel and cameras next to the Pathfinder lander.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft reached Mars wrapped in balloons and bounced like a giant ball. It carried a little wheeled robot that weighed about as much as a big cat, around 10 kilos. Where would you send it first?
texto.org: Mars Pathfinder, landing on Jul 4, 1997 at 19.095 N, 33.253 W (Ares Vallis) with an airbag system; the lander (Carl Sagan Memorial Station) and the Sojourner rover operated until Sep 1997. Coordinates: PDS Geosciences Node; Sojourner listed among the inactive spacecraft by Kilic 2022.

faq.ninos: Yes, both of them: the big spacecraft and the little robot, which stayed close to it.
faq.org: Both inactive since Sep 1997; the lander, its airbags and the heat shield have been identified in MRO HiRISE images.

faq.ninos: It showed that a robot can move around on Mars by itself. Bigger robots came afterwards.
faq.org: It demonstrated airbag landing and the operation of an autonomous rover, technology reused by Spirit and Opportunity in 2004.

marte-mars-polar-lander.nombre: Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2 probes
marte-mars-polar-lander.objeto: Polar lander and two impact microprobes (Deep Space 2)
marte-mars-polar-lander.casi_fallo: The most likely cause: when the legs deployed, a sensor gave a false touchdown signal and the software shut the engines off about 40 metres up.
marte-mars-polar-lander.leccion: Test the complete landing sequence exactly as it will fly; one unrehearsed detail can lose the whole mission.
marte-mars-polar-lander.logro: It was going to dig at the south pole looking for ice; its loss changed the way NASA tests and reviews its landings.
marte-mars-polar-lander.por_que_termino: It crashed during descent or landing.
marte-mars-polar-lander.nota: Lost during descent; position read from a HiRISE map.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft was going to dig at the pole of Mars, but a sensor got confused and shut the engines off when it was still 40 metres up, like a 12-storey building. Nobody has found it. Where do you think it fell?
texto.org: Mars Polar Lander, loss of contact on Dec 3, 1999 during descent over 76.57 S, 165.2 E (Planum Australe); it carried the Deep Space 2 microprobes. Probable cause: premature engine shutdown due to a spurious signal from the leg sensors. Site not identified; planned coordinates according to Lakdawalla's map, The Planetary Society.

faq.ninos: It is surely somewhere at the south pole, but nobody has seen where.
faq.org: Whereabouts unknown. Searches with MGS and HiRISE have not confirmed any candidate; the Deep Space 2 probes did not transmit either.

faq.ninos: That you have to rehearse the whole landing, not just each part separately.
faq.org: The Review Board report (2000) found that the touchdown sensor logic was not tested with leg deployment; it led to independent reviews and integrated testing for Phoenix.

marte-beagle-2.casi_fallo: It landed well, but two of its solar panels did not open and covered the antenna: it could never call home.
marte-beagle-2.leccion: A small mechanism that does not open can silence an entire mission; they must be tested many times.
marte-beagle-2.logro: It was given up for lost for 11 years, until in 2015 it turned up in orbital photos, intact and partially deployed.
marte-beagle-2.por_que_termino: It was left inactive on the Martian surface.

texto.ninos: This little spacecraft reached Mars on Christmas Day, but two of its petals did not open and it could not say it had arrived. People searched for it for 11 years, longer than many people in your class have been alive, until they saw it in a photo. What would you say to it if you could talk to it?
texto.org: Beagle 2 (ESA/United Kingdom), landing on Dec 25, 2003 at ~11.5 N, 90.4 E (Isidis Planitia); incomplete panel deployment blocked the antenna. Located in HiRISE images in 2015. Coordinates: Lakdawalla's map, The Planetary Society; status: Kilic 2022 (inactive).

faq.ninos: Yes, whole and still. From above it looks like a flower with half-open petals.
faq.org: Inactive since landing. Identified in MRO HiRISE images (Jan 2015) with at least two panels undeployed.

faq.ninos: Its solar panels were also its lid, and because they did not open all the way, the antenna stayed covered.
faq.org: The radio antenna sat under the panels; without full deployment there was no line of sight to Mars Express or Mars Odyssey.

marte-spirit.estado: Inactive (stuck in soft sand; last contact in March 2010)
marte-spirit.casi_fallo: Three weeks after arriving, a memory problem left it rebooting non-stop; in 2009 it got stuck in loose sand and could not angle its panels towards the Sun.
marte-spirit.leccion: Terrain is deceptive: a firm crust can hide soft sand underneath.
marte-spirit.logro: Planned for 90 days, it worked for more than 6 years and found almost pure silica, a sign of ancient hot springs.
marte-spirit.por_que_termino: It was left inactive on the Martian surface.
marte-spirit.nota: Coordinates of the landing site, not of where it ended up.
marte-spirit.historia: Designed for a lifetime of 90 Martian days, it explored Gusev crater and the Columbia Hills for more than six years.
marte-spirit.legado_cientifico: It found evidence of hydrothermal activity and of water in Mars's past, including deposits of almost pure silica.
marte-spirit.equipo_dejado: Dust-covered rover, with camera mast, robotic arm and rock abrasion tool.

texto.ninos: This robot was meant to last 3 months and worked for more than 6 years, like a toy that never wears out. In the end it got stuck in sand and fell asleep. What name would you give its final spot?
texto.org: Spirit (MER-A), landing on Jan 4, 2004 at 14.571892 S, 175.47848 E (Gusev crater); last contact on Mar 22, 2010, stuck at Troy next to Home Plate. The coordinates are those of the landing site, not the rover's final position (declared data bias). Source: PDS Geosciences Node / Lakdawalla's map; status: Kilic 2022.

faq.ninos: Yes, stuck in the sand about 7 kilometres from where it landed.
faq.org: Inactive since Mar 2010; it travelled 7.73 km. The final position (Troy, ~14.6 S, 175.5 E) differs from the landing point shown here.

faq.ninos: It is history: it found clues that there was hot water on Mars a long time ago.
faq.org: Kilic (2022) considers the inactive rovers historic relics; its hydrothermal silica findings remain a reference in the search for past habitability.

marte-opportunity.estado: Inactive (lost contact during a global dust storm in June 2018)
marte-opportunity.casi_fallo: In 2005 it was buried up to its axles in a dune for six weeks; in 2018 a global dust storm blocked out the Sun and it never woke up.
marte-opportunity.leccion: What ends a mission may be the weather, not a failure: you have to plan for dust.
marte-opportunity.logro: It travelled more than 45 km in 14 years, a record beyond Earth, and found minerals formed in water.
marte-opportunity.por_que_termino: It was left inactive on the Martian surface.
marte-opportunity.nota: Coordinates of the landing site, not of where it ended up.
marte-opportunity.historia: It landed in Meridiani Planum and operated for almost 15 Earth years, travelling more than 45 km, far beyond its 90-day mission.
marte-opportunity.legado_cientifico: It found conclusive proof of acidic liquid water in the past, such as the hematite 'blueberries' and sulphate deposits.
marte-opportunity.equipo_dejado: Rover with dust-covered solar panels, camera mast and robotic arm, in Perseverance Valley (Endeavour crater).

texto.ninos: This robot travelled more than 45 kilometres across Mars, like a whole marathon, over 14 years. A dust storm blocked out the Sun and it ran out of power. What would you say to it when the Sun comes out again?
texto.org: Opportunity (MER-B), landing on Jan 25, 2004 at 1.9483 S, 5.52583 W (Eagle crater, Meridiani Planum); last contact on Jun 10, 2018 during the global dust storm. The coordinates are those of the landing site; the final position is Perseverance Valley, on the rim of Endeavour crater (declared data bias). Source: PDS Geosciences Node / Lakdawalla's map; status: Kilic 2022.

faq.ninos: Yes, on the slope of a big crater, far from where it landed.
faq.org: Inactive since Jun 2018; mission declared over on Feb 13, 2019. Total traverse 45.16 km; final position in Perseverance Valley, not at the point shown.

faq.ninos: Little mineral balls that only form with water. Mars was wet long ago.
faq.org: Hematite spherules and layered sulphates, evidence of acidic liquid water in the past of Meridiani Planum.

marte-phoenix.estado: Inactive (out of power when the Arctic winter arrived, November 2008)
marte-phoenix.casi_fallo: It reused the design of the lost Mars Polar Lander; the full sequence of legs and engines had to be tested again before flying.
marte-phoenix.leccion: A well-studied failure can become a success: Phoenix flew with the corrections from 1999.
marte-phoenix.logro: It confirmed water ice just under the ground in the Martian Arctic and saw it snow.
marte-phoenix.por_que_termino: It was left inactive on the Martian surface.
marte-phoenix.nota: It dug up water ice near the north pole.
marte-phoenix.historia: It landed on the Arctic plain of Vastitas Borealis and dug into the ground with a robotic arm to reach the buried ice.
marte-phoenix.legado_cientifico: It confirmed the presence of water ice under the surface and detected perchlorates in Martian soil.
marte-phoenix.equipo_dejado: Fixed platform with circular solar panels and a robotic arm.

texto.ninos: This spacecraft dug in the north of Mars and found ice just 5 centimetres down, less than the length of your finger. Then winter came and it fell asleep forever. What would you do with ice from Mars?
texto.org: Phoenix, landing on May 25, 2008 at 68.22 N, 125.75 W (Vastitas Borealis); it confirmed subsurface water ice. Last contact on Nov 2, 2008; damaged by winter CO2 ice. Coordinates: PDS Geosciences Node; status: Kilic 2022 (inactive).

faq.ninos: Yes, but the winter ice broke its solar panels.
faq.org: Inactive since Nov 2008; HiRISE images from 2010 show the solar panels collapsed under the load of CO2 ice.

faq.ninos: That there is frozen water under the ground and that snow falls on Mars.
